### Batch-Level Findings

Official B1 admissions sources strongly favour **class-based and workshop-based assessment** over purely repertory-led judging. Ballet schools repeatedly use preliminary class/audition stages, often followed by finals or callbacks, while contemporary-led programmes more often use admissions workshops, improvisation, dialogue and interview. citeturn6view0turn10view12turn8view0turn16search1turn16search0turn14search1turn4view0

The most repeated B1 audition components are: ballet and/or contemporary classwork, solo presentation, improvisation or creative task, interview or reflective conversation, and in several schools a two-stage process that separates initial video or preliminary screening from later live assessment. This is particularly clear at Rambert, ENBS, Central, LCDS, Juilliard and USC Kaufman. citeturn6view0turn10view13turn19view0turn19view1turn16search1turn16search0turn14search1turn4view0

B1 provides useful but uneven style coverage. Ballet is the strongest area, supported by Royal Ballet School, ENBS, Central, Elmhurst and Rambert; contemporary is also well covered through NSCD, Trinity Laban and LCDS. Jazz/commercial evidence is thinner in official admissions sources, but London Studio Centre and Urdang give the clearest public signals, and USC Kaufman adds hip-hop/freestyle at live-final stage. Tap appears mainly as an allowed solo genre at LSC video stage rather than a fully described assessment framework. citeturn10view14turn10view12turn19view0turn10view6turn6view0turn18search0turn8view0turn16search1turn11view2turn15search1turn4view0

Video submission and assessability requirements are much clearer in a minority of B1 sources than in others. Central and USC Kaufman are particularly strong on full-body visibility, stable camera, limited editing and route-specific content. London Studio Centre gives very strong pathway-by-pathway tape tasks, while Urdang gives content requirements for first-round video auditions. Elmhurst and ENBS confirm video as a screening route but give less public detail about how the video itself is assessed. citeturn7view0turn15search14turn4view1turn11view2turn15search1turn15search4turn9view5

Training potential versus current level is one of the strongest recurring B1 themes. Rambert, NSCD, Central, Bird, ENBS and Trinity Laban explicitly frame admissions around both present demonstration and potential to develop, rather than only current polish. citeturn6view0turn18search0turn19view0turn2view0turn17search7turn8view0

Accessibility and fairness language is present but uneven. NSCD, Bird, Rambert and LCDS give the clearest wording on disability disclosure, reasonable adjustments, widening participation, support needs and non-discrimination. These are valuable B1 anchors for later non-penalisation work. citeturn18search0turn2view0turn6view1turn16search1

B1 also helps separate **tape-observable** from **live-room-only** evidence. Full-body framing, stable camera, lack of editing overlays, and route-specific movement content are tape-observable; responsiveness to in-room guidance, physical examinations, workshop discussion, physio checks and some interviews are inherently live-only or partly live-only. citeturn4view1turn19view0turn19view1turn4view0turn10view13turn2view0

### Evidence Gaps Discovered in B1

B1 leaves several important gaps for later batches:

- **Tap-specific public criteria** remain very thin; B1 mainly shows tap as an allowable solo style, not a detailed assessment framework.  
- **Jazz and commercial/street criteria** are present but concentrated in relatively few sources, especially London Studio Centre and Urdang.  
- **Hip-hop-specific formal public criteria** are sparse; USC includes hip-hop in live finals, but not a detailed rubric.  
- **Exam-board and adjudication descriptors** are still missing; B1 is admissions-heavy, not formal assessment-framework-heavy.  
- **Accessibility-safe assessment standards** appear in policy language, but not yet in a dance-technique-specific observable framework.  
- **Tape-observable vs live-room-only distinctions** are clearer than baseline, but still inconsistent across schools.  
- **Choreography pick-up / learning speed** appears in some sources indirectly, but still needs fuller formal backing.  
- **Stamina overclaim risk** is not specifically addressed in most B1 sources.  
- **Dance-only category labelling** is not addressed in B1 public admissions pages.  
- **ABT coverage remains unresolved** because the two listed ABT pages were inaccessible in this run.

## Reusable Handoff Pack

### DANCE-B1 handoff summary

DANCE-B1 is complete at extraction level and is strongest where schools publish either an official audition pack/policy PDF or a linked criteria document. The highest-confidence B1 evidence comes from Rambert, NSCD, ENBS, Central School of Ballet, Bird College, London Studio Centre, USC Kaufman and, to a slightly lesser extent, Trinity Laban and LCDS. Across these sources, the recurring admissions model is: preliminary screening through classwork or video, followed by a more detailed live stage involving technique classes, solo work, improvisation/creative tasks and often interview. Ballet schools lean heavily on class-based observation, pointe/technique splits and potential for professional training. Contemporary-led schools lean more strongly into workshop tasks, improvisation, creative response, dialogue and wider readiness for a portfolio career.

The most important B1 non-regression evidence for later Dance work is about **assessability**. Central and USC Kaufman explicitly require full-body visibility, stable framing, minimal editing and enough proximity for technique and musicality to be seen. London Studio Centre gives the clearest style-specific video task breakdown across ballet, contemporary and jazz/commercial. Urdang confirms first-round auditions by video with contrasting dance solos. At the same time, several sources reserve parts of assessment for live interaction only: interviews, responsiveness to direction, physio checks, physical examinations, seminar-style discussion or workshop adaptation.

Fairness and accessibility are also present in B1. NSCD, Bird, Rambert and LCDS all publish support/adjustment or non-discrimination language tied directly to admissions. This is important because later Dance audit/revision work will need to distinguish legitimate assessability issues from unlawful or unsafe inference about disability, injury history, body presentation or production value.

## Batch-level findings

Across entity["organization","Royal Academy of Dance","dance body uk"] and entity["organization","Imperial Society of Teachers of Dancing","dance body uk"], the strongest formal frameworks recur around **technique/body organisation**, **musical response**, and **performance communication**. RAD is especially clear on **posture/weight placement**, **coordination**, **control**, **line**, **spatial awareness**, **timing**, **responsiveness to music**, **expression**, **projection**, **interpretation** and **communication**. ISTD contemporary, modern theatre and tap then deepen that picture with form-specific language around **breath**, **drop and suspension of weight**, **style/theme**, **use of space**, **line/style**, **clarity of beating** and **rhythmic interpretation**. citeturn20view1turn20view2turn23view0turn16view2turn13view1turn6view9turn16view4

Ballet-specific evidence in B2 is strongest through RAD and the two ballet-heavy competition sources. RAD gives the densest formal descriptor language. entity["organization","Prix de Lausanne","dance competition switzerland"] adds artistry, musical sensitivity, dynamics, technical facility, control and coordination, but it also includes **physical suitability**, which is clearly competition/scouting language and should not be normalised into a general dance-audition rubric. entity["organization","Youth America Grand Prix","ballet competition us"] adds category structure, repertoire rules, and finals thresholds, but far less direct technique-descriptor language than RAD. citeturn20view1turn20view0turn6view11turn18view2turn18view0

Contemporary and modern criteria are much richer after B2 than they were after B1. ISTD contemporary supports **alignment**, **weight**, **breath**, **quality/flow**, **space**, **structured improvisation**, and **presentation**, while ISTD modern theatre adds **dynamic and rhythmic awareness**, **projection**, **style/theme**, and examiner-set improvisation/unset sequence work. This is important because it shows that contemporary-led feedback should often be more precise than generic “control” and should distinguish body organisation, musicality, performance and improvisational/creative response. citeturn23view0turn6view6turn13view1turn16view3

Jazz-adjacent and tap coverage also improved materially. Modern Theatre’s Jazz Awards explicitly separate **jazz technique**, **line**, **style**, **timing and musicality**, **use of space**, **knowledge of syllabus**, **sense of performance** and routine work. Tap is even more concrete, separating **posture**, **clarity of beating**, **precision of footwork**, **timing and rhythmic interpretation**, **line/style**, **response/knowledge** and **sense of performance**, while also showing where live examiner prompts matter. citeturn13view1turn6view9turn23view1

Street and hip-hop evidence remains useful but more competition-conditioned than the exam-board ballet/contemporary/tap material. ISTD street stresses **groove**, **freestyle vs choreography**, music understanding and cultural/style grounding. HHI then gives very explicit adjudication language for **creativity**, **showmanship**, **musicality**, **synchronization**, **variety of dance styles**, and — crucially for assessability — **continuous head-to-toe choreography** and a **clear unobstructed head-to-toe view** for judges. IDO further shows that tap, jazz, show and hip-hop are treated as genuinely different adjudication systems, not one generic dance standard. citeturn24view0turn17view0turn16view9turn12view0turn16view8

Accessibility and reasonable-adjustment language is strongest in RAD and ISTD, not in the competition sources. Both organisations explicitly protect standards while allowing process adjustments, and both frame adjustments as ways to remove barriers so dancers can demonstrate required attainment. That is directly relevant to later Dance audit/revision work because it supports **non-penalisation** and rejects simplistic inferences from disability, injury, or adapted process. citeturn9view0turn17view2turn16view5

B2 is materially weaker on pure self-tape guidance than B1. The clearest B2 recorded-evidence sources are Prix de Lausanne’s **video selection** contents and U.DANCE’s **stage vs screen** strand separation. HHI is still valuable because it demands **head-to-toe visibility** and warns that over-edited music can hurt phrasing and musicality, but it is not a self-tape standard as such. citeturn16view6turn18view3turn16view9turn12view1

The largest “do not import directly” finding is that several sources publish formal percentages or system rules that are meaningful **inside those source environments only**: RAD attainment bands and pass rules; ISTD tap/jazz mark allocations; YAGP finals thresholds; IDO 3D/4D/X’ing systems; and HHI’s 50/50 performance-skill split. These are valid comparator evidence, but they are **not** TapeCoach scoring logic. citeturn20view2turn13view1turn19view9turn16view8turn16view9

## Evidence gaps discovered in B2

- **Admissions-to-exam/competition transferability remains a live gap.** B2 is now strong on formal descriptors, but many of its strongest sources are still exam-board or competition frameworks rather than audition decision frameworks. That means later synthesis must distinguish “good comparator language” from “directly transferable audition criteria”. citeturn20view1turn16view9turn6view11
- **Jazz is improved, but still partly proxy-covered through Modern Theatre and competition rules.** B2 now has strong jazz-adjacent language in ISTD Modern Theatre and some jazz/show distinctions in IDO, but it is still thinner on standalone public jazz-audition frameworks than on ballet/contemporary/tap. citeturn13view1turn16view8
- **Commercial/street/hip-hop evidence remains predominantly competition-specific.** ISTD street gives cultural/foundational context and HHI gives explicit criteria, but much of the explicit language is still battle/championship oriented. citeturn24view0turn17view0turn16view9
- **Tape-observable versus live-room-only distinctions are still uneven.** Prix and U.DANCE are helpful for video/submission framing, but most B2 sources still assume exam rooms, live competition floors, or DJ/judge interaction rather than normal self-tape conditions. citeturn16view6turn18view3turn17view0turn16view9
- **Choreography pick-up / learning speed remains patchy.** ISTD contemporary and modern theatre have examiner-set improvisation/unset sequence evidence, and YAGP workshops mention observing how students apply new information, but this remains much less robust than core technique/musicality domains. citeturn6view6turn13view1turn17view4
- **Stamina overclaim risk remains unresolved.** HHI and some competition sources value continuous dynamic performance, but B2 does not provide a clean, accessibility-safe, tape-only standard for stamina inference. citeturn13view2turn16view9
- **Production-value versus assessability boundaries are still only partially covered.** YAGP’s “basic dance clothing is not deducted”, HHI’s warning about over-edited music, and U.DANCE’s no-prestige weighting around choreography creation help, but B2 does not yet provide a full cross-style self-tape standard for production-value bias. citeturn17view4turn12view1turn21view0
- **Dance-only category labelling remains a gap.** B2 gives formal dance domains but does not solve the existing user-facing “vocal” proxy problem in the current baseline. That remains a later audit/revision matter, not a B2 extraction answer.

### Reusable handoff pack for DANCE-B3

**DANCE-B2 handoff summary**  
DANCE-B2 is complete at extraction level and materially strengthens the Dance branch in three areas. First, it gives the branch a formal descriptor base from exam-board sources, especially RAD and ISTD. RAD’s strongest contribution is a reusable domain set around posture/weight placement, coordination, control, line, spatial awareness, timing, responsiveness to music, expression, projection, interpretation and communication. ISTD then adds technique-specific depth: contemporary contributes breath, weight, alignment, flow, space and structured improvisation; modern theatre/jazz-adjacent material contributes musicality, projection, style/theme, line, use of space and presentational skills; tap contributes clarity of beating, rhythmic interpretation, footwork precision and audible response. citeturn20view1turn23view0turn13view1turn6view9

Second, B2 improves the fairness baseline. RAD and ISTD both make clear that reasonable adjustments should remove barriers without changing standards or giving unfair advantage, and that candidates remain assessed against the required attainment. This is important for later audit/revision because it supports accessibility-safe assessment and helps separate legitimate process adaptation from unlawful or unsafe inference about disability, injury, stamina or non-standard presentation. citeturn9view0turn17view2turn16view5

Third, B2 narrows the style gap for street/hip-hop and competition language, but mostly through competition frameworks rather than admissions. HHI is especially valuable for head-to-toe visibility, synchronization, musical phrasing, authenticity of style and full-body choreography. IDO helps show that jazz, show, tap and hip-hop are adjudicated through genuinely different systems. Prix, YAGP and U.DANCE add useful comparator evidence for video-selection contents, category structure, costume non-penalisation and stage-vs-screen distinctions, but these remain competition or platform specific rather than direct audition standards. citeturn16view9turn16view8turn16view6turn17view4turn18view3

## Practitioner and Professional Criteria Added Beyond Formal Frameworks

B3 adds **official professional-process evidence** that B1 and B2 did not fully cover. The clearest official additions are: a **video-first professional company call** with explicit reel length, partnering, technical range and company-specific stylistic expectations from Martha Graham; **callback/open-to-direction evidence** from Disney’s official audition FAQ; and a professional-company **safe and inclusive recruitment** signal from Rambert. Together, these strengthen the Dance branch’s ability to distinguish what can be inferred from a submitted video from what belongs to later live or callback stages. citeturn9view0turn4view5turn4view0

B3 also adds **commercial-process evidence** that sits outside exam-board language. The strongest practitioner additions are speed-learning, camera literacy, slate readiness, freestyle/improvisation under pressure, and style-specific research on a choreographer, artist or show. Those themes recur in Dance Magazine and Backstage, even though both remain lower-authority than official admissions or exam-board documents. citeturn12view0turn10view0turn10view1turn10view2

Just as importantly, B3 surfaces several things that should **not** become scoring criteria. Dance Magazine explicitly discusses image, follower count, and casting-market logic in commercial contexts; Broadway Dance Center prep pages include beauty tips, hair/makeup and what-to-wear coaching for dance-team auditions. Those are useful as **exclusion flags** and as evidence of what not to overgeneralise into a dance-assessment rubric. citeturn12view0turn12view1turn3view7turn3view8

## Batch-Level Findings and Evidence Gaps

### Batch-Level Findings

The official company / professional evidence in B3 is relatively thin but still useful. Rambert contributes inclusion and safe-recruitment language rather than movement standards; Martha Graham contributes the clearest official company audition specification in the batch; Disney contributes broad but useful official performer-audition preparation and callback-direction expectations. citeturn4view0turn9view0turn4view5

Commercial / theatre / practitioner guidance is stronger on **process demands** than on formal assessment domains. Dance Magazine and Backstage both highlight speed-learning, research into choreographer/style, comfort on camera, freestyle readiness, and preparation for long audition days. Those themes are professionally useful for later report language, but they are not robust enough to stand alone as formal scoring anchors without corroboration from stronger source types. citeturn12view0turn10view0turn10view1turn10view2

Direction-taking and adaptability are much clearer in B3 than in B1/B2, but still mostly as **live-room or callback evidence** rather than finished-tape evidence. Disney explicitly says candidates should be open to direction in a callback; Backstage and Dance Magazine stress quick learning and response to professional demands, but largely as process skills. Martha Graham’s staged process, from video reel to invited in-person round, also supports the distinction between what a reel can show and what a later stage can test. citeturn4view5turn10view0turn12view0turn9view0

Professional presentation versus marketability/polish boundaries are still only partly resolved. B3 confirms that on-camera work and basic profile readiness matter in some commercial contexts, but it also shows how quickly professional-prep advice drifts into image, follower count, fashion, or beauty logic. That makes B3 especially useful for **negative design rules**: do not reward expensive production polish, social following, beauty advice or market-facing image as though they were dance skill. citeturn4view5turn12view0turn12view1turn3view8

### Evidence Gaps Discovered in B3

Several gaps remain after B3. Commercial / street / hip-hop evidence outside competition is still thin and depends heavily on practitioner or prep-class sources instead of high-authority formal frameworks. Theatre-dance expectations remain present only in broad performer/company or commercial-prep language, rather than a robust dance-only descriptor set. Tap remains much stronger in B2 exam-board material than in professional B3 sources. citeturn12view0turn10view0turn3view8

Choreography pick-up / learning speed is better represented in B3, but still largely as **live-room or process evidence** rather than something that can be safely inferred from a finished self-tape. Access and non-penalisation language in professional audition contexts also remains thin: Rambert and Martha Graham supply inclusion statements, but neither publishes the same level of detailed adjustment/process boundary language seen in RAD/ISTD. Production-value versus assessability boundaries in professional dance tapes also remain under-specified. citeturn4view0turn9view0turn10view0turn12view0

Stamina overclaim boundaries, dance-only category labelling, and sharply defined tape-observable versus live-room-only distinctions are still not complete enough to close the branch confidently without either a targeted B4 pass or explicit synthesis limitations. citeturn10view3turn10view4turn4view5turn9view0

## DANCE-B4 Decision

**DANCE-B4 appears required.**

The reason is that B3 improves professional-process coverage, but it does **not** fully close several essential evidence gaps. The Dance branch still lacks sufficiently strong non-competition evidence for commercial / street / hip-hop assessment outside practitioner journalism and prep-class culture; still lacks strong self-tape / video-assessability sources specific to professional dance beyond a few indirect signals; still lacks robust accessibility-safe movement assessment and non-penalisation guidance in professional or company contexts; and still lacks stronger handling of production-value versus assessability, stamina overclaim boundaries, and choreography pick-up evidence that can be separated cleanly into tape-observable versus live-room-only domains. citeturn12view0turn10view0turn10view1turn4view0turn9view0

Those gaps are not merely optional refinements. They affect whether later Dance synthesis can speak with enough confidence about commercial/street subtypes, accessibility-safe self-tape assessment, and what should or should not be inferred from a dance tape. Some limitations could be carried into synthesis, but the remaining gaps are substantial enough that a bounded B4 pass is justified before DANCE-SYN.

A DANCE-B4 ledger was **not** supplied in this prompt, so no B4 rows are invented.

## Reusable Handoff Pack

### DANCE-B3 handoff summary

DANCE-B3 is complete at extraction level and adds useful professional-context evidence, but it is much weaker than B1 and B2 in terms of formal descriptor strength. Its strongest official source is Martha Graham’s 2026 company audition call, which clearly separates a first-round video reel from a later in-person stage and explicitly names technical range, ballet, some Graham experience and partnering as requirements. Disney’s official audition FAQ is also useful because it makes callback openness to direction explicit, ties dancer preparation to role-specific clothing/shoe expectations, and confirms that profile materials and video links can matter in official professional processes. Rambert’s company page adds professional inclusion and safe-recruitment language, but not movement criteria.

The practitioner/trade sources are most useful where they fill professional-process gaps that exam boards do not address well. Dance Magazine and Backstage both reinforce speed-learning, on-camera translation, freestyle/improvisation, choreographer/style research, and the practical demands of long commercial audition days. However, these sources also show why later Dance work must be careful: they mix useful performance-process language with market/image logic, including follower counts, photo “looks”, hair/makeup advice and other casting-preference signals that should not become rubric criteria. The Broadway Dance Center prep pages are even clearer examples of this boundary. They are useful as process/context comparators for dance-team and commercial-sport auditions, but they do not provide formal evaluative criteria.

Overall, B3 narrows the gap on callback direction, choreography pickup, commercial camera awareness and professional prep culture, but it does not fully resolve commercial/street/hip-hop assessment outside competition, accessibility-safe professional audition assessment, or production-value versus assessability boundaries. Those remaining gaps are serious enough that B4 is warranted before synthesis.

## Readiness and search strategy

**1. B4 Readiness and Scope Check**

The required handoff context for DANCE-B1, DANCE-B2 and DANCE-B3 was present in the prompt. The B3 handoff explicitly stated that **DANCE-B4 appears required**. A DANCE-B4 ledger was **not supplied**, so this run conducted a **bounded B4 source discovery and extraction pass** only. New B4 IDs begin at **DANCE-S064**. This run does **not** synthesise the whole Dance discipline and does **not** produce rubric revision, scoring changes, implementation changes, or code.  

**2. Search Strategy and Source Selection**

The search was bounded to nine specific gap areas: stronger commercial/street/hip-hop evidence outside competition; direct professional dance-video/self-tape assessability; accessibility-safe movement assessment; non-penalisation/access in professional dance contexts; production-value versus assessability; choreography pick-up/learning-speed; stamina/fatigue overclaim boundaries; theatre/commercial dance evidence outside marketability logic; and whether any remaining evidence should block DANCE-SYN. Searches prioritised official company audition pages, official professional entertainment audition portals, official union/casting guidance, and official inclusive dance-company audition notices. This produced a compact source family centred on Candoco, Stopgap, Equity, Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises, NCLH and Princess. citeturn14view0turn6view2turn6view3turn6view4turn21view0turn25view0turn25view1turn25view2turn25view3

Candoco’s current “Work With Us” page was official but contained only vacancy/process context rather than dance-audition criteria. One Dance UK’s “Considering Difference” resource was relevant to accessible dance spaces but was less audition-specific than the stronger Equity/Candoco/Stopgap evidence. Spotlight, Mandy and Casting Networks results were excluded as lower-authority and/or acting-led practitioner guidance outside the bounded B4 need. ### DANCE-S064 — Candoco Dance Company Audition Notice 2024

- **Institution/body/person:** Candoco Dance Company  
- **Verified URL:** https://candoco.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Candoco-Dance-Company-Audition-Notice-2024.pdf  
- **Page/document title actually checked:** *AUDITIONS 2024*  
- **Authority type:** Official professional company  
- **Source type:** Official company audition notice / PDF  
- **Gap targeted:** professional dance-video assessability; accessibility-safe assessment; production-value boundaries; stamina/fatigue caution  
- **Assessment context:** Professional inclusive company recruitment  
- **Final extraction status:** fully extracted: criteria found  
- **Explicit criteria extracted:** Candoco says it is looking for performers “confident adapting and remaking material” and creating from practice and lived experience. Essential criteria are artistry, training, performance awareness, collaboration/allyship, touring capacity with company access support, and availability/commitment. Stage-one application includes a short statement, CV or “mind map”, and a **4-minute video of you dancing**. Candoco states that the video “is not about production values” and may be a smartphone recording; the key use is to understand “the ways you move”. Candoco’s FAQ further says the most useful footage shows technique lineage, improvisational style, and a range of ways the dancer moves. Candoco also states that gaps in CV/training, including convalescence, are “not a problem” and “will not be held against you”. Access support includes BSL-interpreted information sessions, upload support, BSL interpretation, sighted guides, creative audio description, a breakout/rest space and regular breaks. Candoco also explicitly says applicants concerned about energy-limiting impairments should still apply and discuss adjustments, and that alternative working modes are being explored beyond a traditional full-tour model. citeturn13view0turn14view0turn12view0
- **Implied criteria, clearly labelled as implied:** *Implied* — Candoco treats video as a first-stage evidence tool for movement range, lineage and improvisational tendencies rather than as a total judgement of touring stamina or whole-job fit. *Implied* — later live audition and interview stages are where more complex access, touring and working-pattern questions are discussed. citeturn14view0
- **Technique/style coverage:** Cross-technique inclusive; explicitly open from contemporary to breakdancing to bharatanatyam. citeturn12view0
- **Commercial / street / hip-hop / theatre relevance:** Useful mainly for inclusive professional dance and style openness rather than theatre/commercial specificity. Breakdancing is explicitly welcomed as valid footage. citeturn12view0
- **Video/tape-observable criteria:** Technique lineage; improvisational style; range of movement; identifiable dancer in video; 4-minute evidence cap; smartphone footage acceptable; video not judged on production values. citeturn14view0turn12view0
- **Live-room-only, callback-only, workshop-only or company-specific criteria:** Invited live audition day and later online interview; discussion of touring realities and access adjustments happens after first-stage screening. citeturn14view0
- **Choreography pickup / learning-speed evidence:** Confidence adapting/remaking material is explicit. Improvisational style is explicitly requested in footage. Pickup speed itself is not formalised in the written criteria. citeturn13view2turn12view0
- **Stamina / endurance language and overclaim caution:** Candoco acknowledges that touring and technical periods can be intense, but also says energy-limiting impairments should not bar application and should instead trigger adjustment discussion. This supports caution against inferring endurance from a short video alone. citeturn13view2turn14view0
- **Accessibility / inclusion / reasonable-adjustment / non-penalisation language:** Strong. BSL, sighted guides, creative audio description, rest space, regular breaks, access support worker, tailored Access to Work support, and explicit non-penalisation for CV gaps and inaccessible traditional training routes. citeturn14view0turn13view4

- **What is not assessed or should not be overclaimed:** Production value, CV formatting quality, uninterrupted training history, or touring endurance from short video alone. citeturn14view0turn12view0

### DANCE-S066 — Equity Casting Guide for Deaf, Disabled and Neurodiverse Dancers

- **Institution/body/person:** Equity  
- **Verified URL:** https://www.equity.org.uk/advice-and-support/casting-and-auditions/casting-guide-for-deaf-disabled-and-neurodiverse-dancers  
- **Page/document title actually checked:** *Casting guide for deaf, disabled and neurodiverse dancers*  
- **Authority type:** Official union / sector guidance  
- **Source type:** Accessibility and casting guidance  
- **Gap targeted:** accessibility-safe movement assessment; non-penalisation; fatigue/access boundaries  
- **Assessment context:** Dance company casting, audition planning, rehearsal engagement  
- **Final extraction status:** fully extracted: criteria found  
- **Explicit criteria extracted:** The guide advises dance companies to make call-outs accessible in multiple formats, allow varied submission forms (CV, written material, video, voice recording), keep language streamlined, and give sufficient lead time. It explicitly recognises that many disabled artists come through non-traditional routes and asks companies to define the experience/qualities sought beyond degree or “three years’ professional experience”. It recommends that early rounds **could be done digitally** to save time and energy. For auditions, it says companies should ask invited artists about access needs, hold auditions in accessible spaces, provide detailed plans for the day, make warm-up/technique classes accessible, allow enough time for rest and toilet/water breaks, and remember that long or multi-day auditions can be barriers for dancers with fatigue and chronic pain conditions. In choreographic practice it advises open movement language, options for translation of set material, adaptation to artists’ own body/pace of learning, and warns against assuming what a dancer is or is not capable of. It also explicitly says not to ask about medical history unless disclosed for safety reasons. citeturn19view0turn19view2turn19view4turn6view3
- **Implied criteria, clearly labelled as implied:** *Implied* — this source strongly supports separating barrier-removal from lowering standards. *Implied* — it also supports scoring language anchored in movement quality and working practice rather than pathology, body norm, or speculative capability. citeturn19view2turn19view4
- **Technique/style coverage:** Cross-style dance; especially applicable to live technique class, workshop and choreography processes.  
- **Commercial / street / hip-hop / theatre relevance:** Generic across dance sectors rather than style-specific.  
- **Video/tape-observable criteria:** Early digital rounds may be appropriate where they reduce travel/energy costs, but access and equal-opportunity considerations remain central. citeturn19view0
- **Live-room-only, callback-only, workshop-only or company-specific criteria:** Detailed plan-of-day, accessible warm-up/technique class, practical site access, open check-ins and live-room adjustment practices. citeturn19view0turn19view4
- **Choreography pickup / learning-speed evidence:** Strong. The guidance explicitly recommends open choreography, optional translation of set material, and encouraging dancers to use notes/video/voice recording to retain material. This is high-value evidence that “pickup” should not be treated as a single standardised body-norm task. citeturn19view2
- **Stamina / endurance language and overclaim caution:** Strong caution source. Long or multi-day auditions can be barriers for fatigue/chronic pain, meaning endurance cannot safely be treated as a neutral or universally comparable indicator. citeturn19view4
- **Accessibility / inclusion / reasonable-adjustment / non-penalisation language:** Strong and central. citeturn6view3turn19view0turn19view2turn19view4
- **Production-value versus assessability language:** Indirect only. The source is stronger on access, submission format flexibility and non-assumption than on filming setup.  
- **Professionalism or preparation evidence:** Clear expectation that audition teams brief themselves on access requirements in advance and communicate structure clearly. citeturn19view4
- **Criteria that should not become rubric criteria:** Degree ownership, standardised traditional training path, medical history, impairment curiosity, or body-norm assumptions must not become scoring criteria. citeturn19view0turn19view2
- **What is assessed:** Movement quality, collaborative working practice, interpretation of tasks, and other practical artistic capacities consistent with accessible planning.  
- **What is not assessed or should not be overclaimed:** Medical condition, invisible fatigue, or any supposed universal movement norm based on non-disabled assumptions. citeturn19view2turn19view4
- **Rubric/report implication for later synthesis:** One of the strongest cross-style fairness sources in the whole Dance branch.  
- **Confidence:** high  
- **Provenance or alias notes:** None.

### DANCE-S067 — Equity Self-tape & Zoom Auditions Guidance

- **Institution/body/person:** Equity  
- **Verified URL:** https://www.equity.org.uk/advice-and-support/casting-and-auditions/self-tape-zoom-auditions-guidance  
- **Page/document title actually checked:** *Self-tape & Zoom auditions guidance*  
- **Authority type:** Official union / casting guidance  
- **Source type:** Self-tape and accessible-auditions guidance  
- **Gap targeted:** self-tape assessability; production-value boundaries; accessibility in remote auditions  
- **Assessment context:** Performer self-tapes and accessible remote audition practice  
- **Final extraction status:** fully extracted: criteria found  
- **Explicit criteria extracted:** Equity says self-tape requests should provide relevant information about tone/style/creative vision. It states that simplicity is key and performers should not be asked to provide their own props or rearrange their home as though it were a set. It recommends four-day minimum turnarounds for longer scripted first-round tapes, capped material loads, no more than two roles/two scenes/two versions, and it says a reader can be helpful but should not be an absolute requirement. The accessible-auditions section adds that PDFs are inaccessible for many people, materials should be sent in accessible formats and as far in advance as possible, BSL interpreters must be sourced where needed, and self-tape/Zoom recalls may require time-slot adjustments because of fatigue. It also warns that if casting teams ask performers to demonstrate skills pertaining to impairment, they should be specific and honest about what is being asked rather than vaguely requesting “tricks”; asking every person about access requirements is recommended so that access becomes normalised. citeturn20view0turn20view1turn20view3
- **Implied criteria, clearly labelled as implied:** *Implied* — the guidance supports evaluating the performance task, not the set-dressing capacity of the performer’s home environment. *Implied* — it also supports distinguishing role-relevant skill requests from exploitative or vague spectacle requests. citeturn20view0turn20view3
- **Technique/style coverage:** General performing arts self-tape guidance, not dance-style specific.  
- **Commercial / street / hip-hop / theatre relevance:** Useful across theatre/commercial casting processes, but not a dance-technique descriptor source.  
- **Video/tape-observable criteria:** Relevant information should be provided; simplicity should be preserved; no home-set transformation; accessible materials and extra preparation time may be required. citeturn20view0turn20view1turn20view3
- **Live-room-only, callback-only, workshop-only or company-specific criteria:** Reader support, time-slot negotiation and access planning are process features, not movement criteria.  
- **Choreography pickup / learning-speed evidence:** Limited. More useful for preparation-time fairness than for movement pickup descriptors.  
- **Stamina / endurance language and overclaim caution:** Useful. The guide recognises fatigue as a relevant access issue in remote recall scheduling. citeturn20view1turn20view3
- **Accessibility / inclusion / reasonable-adjustment / non-penalisation language:** Strong. citeturn20view1turn20view3
- **Production-value versus assessability language:** Strong. No props/set-building expectation; simplicity is central. citeturn20view0
- **Professionalism or preparation evidence:** Clear direction, realistic time frame, and communication are part of best practice. citeturn6view4turn20view0
- **Criteria that should not become rubric criteria:** Home-set quality, access to readers, ability to source props, bare-nudity requests, or speed under inaccessible deadlines. citeturn20view0turn20view1turn20view2
- **What is assessed:** The task/performance requested, within a fair and accessible process.  
- **What is not assessed or should not be overclaimed:** Production design, home space quality, or lack of access support.  
- **Rubric/report implication for later synthesis:** Strong process-boundary source for production-value versus assessability.  
- **Confidence:** high  
- **Provenance or alias notes:** Related to S068 but not a duplicate; S067 is broader and includes the accessible-auditions section.

### DANCE-S068 — Equity Code of Best Practice for Self-Tape & Zoom Auditions for Commercials

- **Institution/body/person:** Equity / PMA / CPMA / CDG / CDA  
- **Verified URL:** https://www.equity.org.uk/media/hbpofr4q/code-of-best-practice-for-self-tape-zoom-auditions-for-commercials-1.pdf  
- **Page/document title actually checked:** *Code of Best Practice for Self-Tape & Zoom Auditions for Commercials*  
- **Authority type:** Multi-body official industry code  
- **Source type:** Commercial self-tape code / PDF  
- **Gap targeted:** production-value boundaries; commercial self-tape norms; non-penalisation  
- **Assessment context:** Commercial self-tape and Zoom audition process  
- **Final extraction status:** fully extracted: criteria found  
- **Explicit criteria extracted:** The code says simplicity is key, performers should not be required to provide their own props or rearrange their homes as though they were a set, and additional material at recall should be reasonable/relevant/not excessive. It sets a two-day minimum turnaround for commercial self-tapes within normal working days/hours, says readers should not be a hard requirement and should not be self-funded, says recall audition fees should be paid whether live or on Zoom, and states that performers should **only be judged on their performance and not on the quality of equipment available to them**. It also prohibits fully or partially nude self-tapes and says only as many tapes should be called as can be properly considered. citeturn21view0turn23view3turn23view4
- **Implied criteria, clearly labelled as implied:** *Implied* — this is one of the clearest sources against rewarding expensive production polish. *Implied* — it also supports excluding unreasonable material-volume and timing pressures from any conception of “professionalism”. citeturn21view0turn23view4
- **Technique/style coverage:** Commercial casting process rather than dance-technique description.  
- **Commercial / street / hip-hop / theatre relevance:** Strong for commercial audition process fairness.  
- **Video/tape-observable criteria:** Performance is the core judgement unit; equipment quality is explicitly excluded. citeturn23view4
- **Live-room-only, callback-only, workshop-only or company-specific criteria:** Recall material may be requested, and recall fees apply whether live or Zoom. citeturn21view0
- **Choreography pickup / learning-speed evidence:** None.  
- **Stamina / endurance language and overclaim caution:** Indirect only; stronger on unreasonable turnaround expectations than on movement endurance.  
- **Accessibility / inclusion / reasonable-adjustment / non-penalisation language:** Moderately strong through fairness and non-equipment judgement, though less dance-specific than S066.  
- **Production-value versus assessability language:** Very strong. citeturn21view0turn23view4
- **Professionalism or preparation evidence:** Relevant information, basic package only, and normal-hours deadlines. citeturn21view0
- **Criteria that should not become rubric criteria:** Equipment quality, home-set quality, ability to self-fund a reader, nudity compliance, or capacity to deliver inaccessible commercial turnaround. citeturn21view0turn23view4
- **What is assessed:** Performance material requested for the commercial audition. citeturn23view4
- **What is not assessed or should not be overclaimed:** Equipment quality, excessive add-ons, or inaccessible speed. citeturn23view4
- **Rubric/report implication for later synthesis:** One of the cleanest B4 sources for “performance not equipment”.

## Batch-level findings and remaining gaps

**8. Batch-Level Findings**

**Commercial / street / hip-hop evidence outside competition.**  
B4 materially improved this gap. Royal Caribbean now provides current official employer evidence for contemporary, jazz, theatre dance, showgirl and hip-hop in the same professional casting process, with separate hip-hop emphasis on breaking, popping/locking, improv and skills. NCLH strengthens the professional non-competition picture by naming commercial jazz, ballet, contemporary and hip-hop as major training emphases, and Celebrity adds a professional online reel requirement spanning jazz, commercial, contemporary and partnering. Together these sources push commercial/street/hip-hop evidence beyond the competition-heavy B2 set, though they remain employer-shaped rather than universal frameworks. citeturn25view0turn25view1turn25view2

**Professional self-tape / dance-video assessability.**  
B4 is strong here. Candoco explicitly says stage-one video is not about production values and may be smartphone footage. Royal Caribbean says virtual submission videos need not be professionally produced if they are clear. Equity’s general and commercials self-tape guidance both reject home-set transformation, and the commercials code expressly says performers should be judged on performance rather than equipment quality. Celebrity shows what content a professional dance reel is expected to contain, and Candoco adds useful specificity around technique lineage, improvisational style and range of movement. citeturn14view0turn20view0turn23view4turn25view0turn25view1

**Accessibility-safe movement assessment and non-penalisation.**  
This is the strongest B4 addition. Candoco and Stopgap publish concrete dance-specific access arrangements. Equity goes further by treating access as part of the whole creative process: accessible formats, advance materials, accessible technique classes, detailed plans, fatigue-aware scheduling, open movement language, adaptation of material to body and pace of learning, and a ban on medical-history curiosity unless safety requires disclosure. B4 therefore materially stabilises later non-penalisation work. citeturn14view0turn6view2turn19view0turn19view2turn19view4

**Production-value versus assessability.**  
B4 gives unusually clear language here: Candoco says “not about production values”; Royal Caribbean says “not professionally produced” is fine if the material is clear; Equity’s commercial code says performance, not equipment, is what should be judged. This is high-value non-regression evidence against rewarding expensive camera polish. citeturn14view0turn25view0turn23view4

**Choreography pick-up / learning-speed and live-room boundaries.**  
B4 does not create a clean universal descriptor, but it clarifies the split. Royal Caribbean’s virtual route uses learned filmed combinations; Princess and NCLH explicitly rely on live combination learning; Stopgap uses set material plus improvisation and creative tasking. The result is enough evidence to distinguish tape-observable preparation from live-room responsiveness and pickup. citeturn25view0turn25view2turn25view3turn6view2

**Stamina / endurance overclaim boundaries.**  
B4 improves caution more than it creates positive scoring language. Equity explicitly says long or multi-day auditions can be barriers for dancers with fatigue and chronic pain. Candoco explicitly treats energy-limited impairment as an access conversation rather than a reason not to apply. This is useful evidence against overclaiming endurance from short clips or rigid room norms, but it remains a caution field rather than a rich descriptor base. citeturn19view4turn14view0

**Source-type limitations.**  
B4’s commercial/professional evidence is strongest in cruise and touring-entertainment employers. These pages often mix valuable style/process evidence with company-specific role constraints such as heights, silhouettes, attire and ship-travel requirements. Those constraints are important provenance context but must not be turned into general dance scoring criteria. citeturn25view0turn25view1turn25view2turn25view3

**What is useful for later rubric/report language.**  
Useful later language includes: clear-not-polished video; range of movement; technique lineage; improvisational style; style-to-style movement; stage presence tied to physical/emotional expression; partnering; physical acting; live combo learning; access-led audition planning; adaptation to body/pace of learning; and explicit separation between first-stage video evidence and later live/callback evidence. citeturn12view0turn14view0turn19view2turn25view0turn25view1turn25view2turn25view3

**What must not be imported into TapeCoach scoring.**  
Body- or height-specific casting filters, “lean silhouette” language, swimsuit/photo requests, ship-travel logistics, role-specific heel demands, nudity/commercial administration rules, and any employer-specific aesthetic preference must remain source-specific context only. citeturn25view0turn25view1turn23view4

### DANCE-B4 handoff summary

DANCE-B4 is complete at extraction level and closes several important gaps left by B3, especially around professional dance-video assessability, inclusive company audition practice, and non-competition commercial/street/hip-hop evidence. The strongest B4 performance-process sources are Candoco, Equity’s dance and self-tape guidance, Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises and NCLH. Candoco is especially important because it explicitly says first-stage dance video is **not about production values**, may be captured on a smartphone, and should instead reveal how the dancer moves, including technique lineage, improvisational style and range. It also adds high-value non-penalisation evidence by accepting bespoke training pathways, not treating CV gaps or convalescence as negative, and publishing detailed access support. Stopgap reinforces inclusive live audition structure through set material, improvisation and creative tasking with access accommodations. citeturn14view0turn12view0turn6view2

Equity’s two B4 sources are central for process and fairness. The dance casting guide gives the strongest public evidence yet for accessibility-safe movement assessment: accessible formats, advance information, detailed plan-of-day, accessible technique classes, fatigue-aware scheduling, open movement language, adaptation of material to body and pace of learning, and clear warnings against medical-history or capability assumptions. The self-tape guidance and commercials code then provide a robust boundary against production-value bias: keep it simple, do not require props or domestic set transformation, and in commercials judge the **performance** rather than the performer’s equipment. citeturn19view0turn19view2turn19view4turn20view0turn23view4

Commercial and professional style evidence also improved. Royal Caribbean adds current non-competition evidence for contemporary, jazz, theatre dance, showgirl and hip-hop, including breaking/popping-locking and audition improv/tricks, while still allowing a virtual route. Celebrity specifies online reel content across jazz, commercial, contemporary and partnering. NCLH and Princess strengthen the live-room side with multiple-combo learning and short choreography before first cut. Remaining gaps mostly concern how cautiously to word pickup speed, stamina and highly employer-specific commercial criteria during synthesis; they do not block DANCE-SYN. B1, B2 and B3 remain complete. citeturn25view0turn25view1turn25view2turn25view3

## Completion statement

DANCE-B4 extraction complete. Ready for DANCE-SYN.# Lessons Learned from the Dance Branch for Rubric Development

## Core conclusion

The strongest lesson from the Dance branch is that rubric improvement did not come mainly from inventing new scoring theory. It came from making an existing shared system more truthful about what it is already doing, more precise about what it can and cannot judge, and more disciplined about how that judgement appears in user-facing output. The baseline-control pack shows that TapeCoach currently runs on a stable shared architecture: fixed operational score fields, a shared report schema, server-side recomputation, and a two-step evidence-plus-polish pipeline. It also shows that discipline specificity is still expressed mostly through inferred type, weighting, prompt prose and category-note wording rather than through formal subtype rubrics. In that environment, label semantics, evidence anchors, claim-scope rules and renderer behaviour are not cosmetic details; they are part of the rubric itself. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file2

The Dance branch therefore matters beyond Dance. It proves that the right question for a new discipline is not “Can we redesign the rubric from scratch?” but “What specificity, restraint and testability can we add inside the current architecture without destabilising the strongest existing flows?” That is exactly the question the control sheet and baseline audit say the product needs to answer: improve discipline-specific specificity while preserving shared-system stability, evidence-led reporting and non-regression of the protected Musical Theatre flow. fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file0

## What the Dance branch demonstrated

The first important result is that architecture-aware revision works. The baseline audit and reconciliation pack both confirm that the operational six-field system is real, stable and shared, and that `vocal` is explicitly overloaded across singing, speech delivery and dance technique. They also confirm that Dance had the weakest credibility because it lacked a true movement rubric and depended on proxy mapping. The Dance branch improved that situation not by changing fields, but by tightening semantics, guardrails, evidence requirements and output rules around those fields. That is a major process gain: wording-and-guardrail revision can deliver meaningful rubric development when the architecture is fixed. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0

The second result is that a protected regression anchor is essential. The baseline materials repeatedly identify Musical Theatre acting-plus-song as the strongest stabilised flow and specify that it must not regress. That constraint was not an obstacle; it was a design aid. It forced Dance work to become more disciplined, because every proposed improvement had to prove that it would not damage multi-component handling, acting/vocal visibility, timestamp spread or MT weighting stability. This is a portable lesson: every discipline cycle should begin by naming the load-bearing flow that must survive change intact. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3

The third result is that output specificity is the real acceptance standard. The stress test shows that many system weaknesses did not appear as outright scoring failure. They appeared as plausible-but-transferable language, under-anchored casting headlines, generic category notes, over-broad technical comments, thin timestamp coverage and false specificity around brief compliance. In other words, the system could sound competent while still failing the goal of being evidence-led and tape-specific. The Dance branch only became operationally solid once revision outputs were translated into concrete output-specificity rules and preserved test scenarios. That is a fundamental lesson for rubric development: a rubric is not complete when wording is improved; it is complete when the wording has been converted into observable output behaviour and regression tests. fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file2

## What still slowed or weakened the cycle

The biggest drag on confidence was not source quality but display-layer uncertainty. The baseline audit and reconciliation pack both flag that type-aware labels are not fully confirmed, comparison-page label logic is uncertain, and timestamp rendering may be losing information somewhere between evidence generation, validation, persistence and output. The stress test reinforces that uncertainty by noting that UI timestamp mapping appears structurally capable of rendering the array, while real outputs still showed under-production or under-display. This means that, late in the cycle, the team still had to reason about wording without being able to fully verify live display behaviour. That should not become normal. Renderer and label-helper verification need to enter the process earlier. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

A second efficiency loss came from prompt-only logic that was not clearly separated from deterministic logic. The reconciliation pack is explicit that some important behaviour, including parts of brief-adherence weighting and score anchoring, remains prompt-led rather than deterministically recomposed. It also notes that there are no formal score anchor tables in code and that subtype handling is underdeveloped across disciplines. That does not make the current product unusable, but it does make auditability harder. The lesson is not that prompt-led logic is unacceptable; it is that every discipline cycle should identify prompt-dependent logic up front and carry it as a named auditability risk instead of discovering it halfway through the branch. fileciteturn0file3

A third weakness was the absence of live Dance outputs in the final stages. The supplied Dance output-specificity handover correctly carried this forward as a limitation rather than pretending the renderer had been verified. That honesty is a strength. But as a process lesson, it means the next discipline should not rely on synthetic/adversarial QA alone if live renderer verification is realistically obtainable. Synthetic mapping is strong for logic; it is weaker for confirming real label behaviour, comparison-page parity and timestamp rendering. The baseline pack itself already warned that those were open uncertainties. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

## Lessons to institutionalise for future rubric work

The most useful carry-forward lessons are best treated as permanent operating rules rather than Dance-only observations.

| Portable lesson | Why the Dance branch proved it | Carry-forward rule |
|---|---|---|
| Start from baseline reality, not design memory | The reconciliation stage showed that remembered rubric intent and actual implementation were not identical, especially around field overload, prompt-led logic and shared report structure | Begin every new discipline with a reconciliation pass before deep research expands |
| Name a protected anchor before changing anything | Musical Theatre stability made Dance revision safer and more disciplined | Require one explicit non-regression anchor for every discipline |
| Audit field semantics before rubric wording | The overloaded `vocal` field became a core rubric problem, not just a naming problem | Add a mandatory field-semantics and label-risk scan at the start of every branch |
| Treat assessability as a first-order rubric domain | The stress test showed technical/audio comments become generic unless tied to what the tape actually allows the system to judge | Every discipline must define its own assessability preconditions early |
| Separate positive criteria from blocked claims | Dance improved most when it defined not just what to praise, but what must not be inferred from tape | Every discipline needs an explicit “must not claim” set |
| Make accessibility explicit, not ambient | General fairness principles existed already, but Dance needed explicit anti-inference and adaptation-without-deficit wording | Every discipline should include an accessibility-safe interpretation layer in revision |
| Convert revision into behaviour, not prose alone | Dance only became QA-ready once the wording package became an output-specificity and test map | Do not treat revision as complete until it produces concrete output rules and test cases |
| Distinguish renderer verification from rubric logic | Label-helper, comparison-page and timestamp-rendering risks persisted despite strong wording | Require a display-layer verification checklist for every discipline |
| Keep a standing limitation spine | Dance moved forward faster once unresolved issues were carried openly instead of being re-litigated at every stage | Maintain one discipline limitation ledger from first extraction batch to output QA |
| Keep source types distinct | The Dance synthesis only became reliable when admissions, formal descriptors, employer context and fairness/self-tape evidence were not collapsed into one standard | Require source-type separation in research, synthesis and audit |

These lessons follow directly from the documented shared architecture, the lack of formal subtype rubrics, the overloaded score-field semantics, the genericity risks in current outputs, and the unresolved renderer/display uncertainties captured in the baseline-control pack. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file3

## Process changes to adopt before the next discipline

The next discipline should not simply reuse the Dance workflow mechanically. It should reuse the successful parts and harden the weak parts.

| Workflow stage | Change to make mandatory | Why it should now be mandatory | Minimum artefact required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preflight | Baseline-control packet plus reconciliation note | Prevents research from drifting away from actual implementation | Baseline slice, guardrails, control sheet, reconcile note, current output examples if available |
| Research | Source-family plan before batch extraction | Keeps formal descriptors, employer sources, accessibility sources and comparators distinct from the start | Source-family ledger and batch scope rules |
| Synthesis | Descriptor dictionary plus claim-scope table | Forces the branch to define both what can be named and what must remain cautious | Recurring domains, style-specific domains, live-room-only boundaries |
| Audit | Display-layer uncertainty register | Stops UI/renderer risks from remaining invisible until the end | Label risk register, comparison-page risk register, timestamp-render uncertainty note |
| Revision | Dual output: wording package plus QA hooks | Makes revision immediately auditable and testable | Clean revised baseline plus section/change register |
| Final audit | Explicit limitation set and release decision | Prevents soft approval and keeps open issues visible | Accepted changes, accepted-with-limitation changes, residual risk register |
| Output specificity | Adversarial scenario pack and live-output checklist | Converts rubric development into behaviour that can be tested | Scenario pack, rule map, renderer checklist, preserved test clusters |
| Release readiness | Live-output spot audit where possible | Ensures the branch is not only logically strong but actually rendered correctly | Real report examples, comparison-page examples, export examples |

This process adjustment is justified by the documented current-state weaknesses: discipline specificity is underdeveloped, fixed fields carry different meanings by type, type-aware labels are not fully confirmed, timestamps are under-produced or under-verified, and shared report sections can sound specific without being sufficiently grounded. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file3

A particularly important addition for the next discipline is an explicit **field-overload review**. Dance showed that a branch can spend large amounts of effort cleaning symptoms that originate in one overloaded stored field. The next discipline should therefore begin with a short but formal answer to three questions: which stored fields are being repurposed, which user-facing labels those fields may trigger, and which of those semantics are architecture-fixed versus wording-fixable. That one move will make later audit and revision work faster and cleaner. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3

## What this means for rubric development itself

The Dance branch sharpened the product’s real rubric philosophy. The control sheet says the rubric should be brief-aware, audition-type-aware, level-aware, evidence-led, timestamp-grounded, practical and safe from protected-trait judgement. Dance showed what that means in operational terms. It means a rubric is not just a list of scoring areas. It is a combination of five things: what the system is allowed to judge, what evidence it needs before making that judgement, how user-facing labels describe the underlying score semantics, what claims must stay low-confidence or live-room-only, and what language must be blocked to prevent genericity or bias. fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file0

That has two practical implications for future rubric development. First, each discipline should be expected to produce its own **descriptor dictionary** and its own **forbidden-claim map**, even if the stored score fields remain shared. Second, each discipline should be expected to end with an **output-behaviour standard**, not just a revised text pack. In other words, the real rubric is now the combination of baseline wording, evidence rules, display semantics and regression tests. The Dance branch made that visible. The next discipline should start there rather than discover it half-way through. The stress test strongly supports this conclusion because it shows that many failures came from the mismatch between plausible prose and missing evidence anchors, not from obviously broken scoring. fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file3

Another deeper lesson is that architecture constraints should not automatically be framed as blockers. In Dance, the fixed schema was a real limitation, but it also created a useful discipline: it forced the team to distinguish between wording fixes, evidence-boundary fixes, display-risk checks and true architecture backlog. That separation is healthy. The next discipline should preserve it by maintaining three parallel lists from the start: **revisable in wording**, **test-only / verification dependent**, and **architecture-shaped residual risks**. That would have shortened the Dance branch further. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file3

## Readiness gates before the next discipline begins

The next discipline should begin only if the following gates are met.

| Readiness gate | Pass condition | Failure signal |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline reality gate | Baseline slice, guardrails, reconcile note and control sheet are present | Research begins from memory rather than implementation |
| Protected anchor gate | One preserved non-regression flow is named explicitly | Revision work has no stable reference point |
| Field semantics gate | Any overloaded stored fields and label risks are enumerated | Label problems surface only during audit |
| Source-family gate | Planned source families are distinct before extraction begins | Synthesis collapses different source types into one “standard” |
| Evidence-anchor gate | The discipline has a draft evidence-anchor dictionary by synthesis stage | Audit and revision stay too generic |
| Display verification gate | Real output examples are supplied before or during final stages where possible | Final audit cannot confirm labels, comparison naming or rendered note behaviour |
| Limitation spine gate | Open risks are carried forward in one explicit ledger | The same unresolved issue gets rediscovered at each stage |
| Completion gate | “Done” means output-specificity and non-regression mapping, not just revision text | The branch ends with strong prose but weak QA readiness |

These gates are not arbitrary. They answer the exact weaknesses documented in the baseline pack: overloaded categories, discipline leakage, lack of subtype anchors, generic shared sections, timestamp underproduction, uncertain label helpers and the need to preserve the MT anchor while improving other disciplines. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file3

The final lesson is the simplest one. The objective is not to make each discipline branch longer or more elaborate. The objective is to make each branch more **auditable**, more **specific**, and more **product-safe**. The Dance branch improved the rubric because it moved from research to synthesis, from synthesis to bounded audit, from audit to traceable revision, and from revision to output behaviour that can actually be tested. That should now be the default standard before the next discipline starts.# DANCE-S0 Dance Source Census
