## Coverage Summary

The census identified **72 preferred source rows**. Duplicate, superseded and alias URLs were normalised into notes rather than retained as separate countable rows, so the **normalised source count is also 72**. All mandatory named source groups were searched and assigned a census status, and none remain unresolved. Based on the preferred rows, the batch distribution is **36 in DANCE-B1**, **18 in DANCE-B2**, **9 in DANCE-B3**, and **9 in DANCE-B4**.

By source type, the preferred set includes **33 official admissions / conservatoire / school sources**, **8 competition / adjudication frameworks**, **7 exam-board / syllabus / formal assessment frameworks**, **8 accessibility / fairness sources**, **6 self-tape / video-audition sources**, **4 official commercial / professional / casting sources**, **5 practitioner / educator sources**, and **1 pedagogy / technique source**. This gives strong coverage of formal admissions and a credible base for accessibility and filming fairness, while also preserving a separate bucket for practitioner context rather than treating it as formal scoring evidence.

By dance style / context, preferred-source coverage is strongest for **ballet**, **contemporary / modern**, **commercial / street**, and **self-tape / filmed audition** contexts. Coverage is present but thinner for **tap**, **jazz**, and especially **hip-hop** as a formal assessment framework, where public high-authority sources are more competition-led than conservatoire-led. Musical-theatre dance is covered mainly through vocational schools and mixed dance/MT programmes rather than standalone dance-only frameworks.

By assessment context, the strongest public-web evidence base is: **school / conservatoire admissions and auditions**, then **exam / qualification frameworks**, then **competition/adjudication frameworks**, followed by **professional / commercial audition guidance** and **accessibility / safe-practice / assessability** sources. This means later extraction should weight B1 and B2 most heavily for formal criteria, use B3 to improve professional realism and report language, and use B4 to set non-penalisation and tape-assessability guardrails. Key provenance limitations are that some commercial guidance is practitioner-led rather than formal, and some competition frameworks are youth- or genre-specific rather than general dance-audition standards. Relevant but non-retained older versions of YAGP, HHI, IDO, Royal Ballet School and ENBS materials were found and deliberately normalised out as superseded or duplicate context. citeturn23view0turn25view3turn28search0turn17search2turn13search0

## Proposed Batch Plan

**DANCE-B1** covers official schools, conservatoires and admissions and is intentionally the largest batch at **36 sources**. These are the strongest public sources for what schools actually ask dancers to do, show or submit, and they are the richest evidence base for tape-observable criteria, admissions workshops, video routes and training-potential language.

**DANCE-B2** covers exam boards, syllabi, adjudication and formal assessment frameworks at **18 sources**. This batch is where technique language, progression structures, explicit criteria, reasonable-adjustment boundaries and competition evaluation descriptors are most likely to be extractable in a disciplined way.

**DANCE-B3** covers commercial, theatre, practitioner and professional guidance at **9 sources**. It is smaller because public high-authority sources here are thinner and more heterogeneous. These sources are valuable for professional expectations and language, but they must not automatically be turned into scoring criteria.

**DANCE-B4** covers technique, accessibility, self-tape and gap-fill sources at **9 sources**. This batch is reserved for sources that are crucial for fairness, non-penalisation, assessability and filmed-dance evidence, especially where formal admissions pages do not say enough about framing, accessible practice or safe dance space.

High-priority placement decisions: admissions-embedded video pages such as Central, London Studio Centre, USC Kaufman and Urdang were kept in **B1** because they are part of official entry criteria, even though they also inform self-tape practice. By contrast, **Arden**, **Mountview** and **GSA** were kept in **B4** because they are most useful as generic or transferable filmed-audition guidance rather than core dance-admissions frameworks. **RAD** and **ISTD** accessibility-adjustment documents were kept in **B2**, not B4, because they are attached to formal assessment systems and later extraction will need to preserve the distinction between changing process and changing criteria. **Rambert** appears in both school and company form: the **Rambert School** admissions sources remain in B1, while the **Rambert company auditions** page is placed in B3 because it reflects professional hiring rather than training admissions. citeturn18search0turn7search15turn13search7turn16search4turn21search1

## Source Alias and Normalisation Notes

The preferred **Royal Academy of Dance** sources use both `royalacademyofdance.org` and `assets.royalacademyofdance.org`. These are treated as one source family; asset-hosted PDFs are not double-counted against the organisation’s main site. citeturn23view0turn26view1

**Urdang** is publicly represented across `theurdang.london`, `urdang.citystgeorges.ac.uk`, and `citystgeorges.ac.uk`. The preferred admissions source is the dedicated Urdang admissions page, with the City course page retained only where it adds distinct track or degree detail. The Urdang homepage itself was not double-counted as a separate substantive source. citeturn6search0turn6search4turn6search9

**ISTD** materials exist both on umbrella landing pages and as direct document URLs under `/documents/`. The landing pages and individual PDFs are only both retained where they serve different functions: the hub page for current-document discovery, and the PDF for likely extractable criteria. Older document versions found in search results were not retained as separate preferred rows. citeturn9search0turn15search1turn15search2turn15search7

For **ENBS** and **The Royal Ballet School**, general landing pages, dated audition pages and detailed packs/guides were normalised so that the most current and detailed pages are preferred. Older or more general pages were used only for verification, not duplicate counting. citeturn1search4turn1search5turn23view2

For **YAGP**, **IDO** and **HHI**, older manuals and prior-year rules appeared in search results, but only the freshest clearly current versions were retained as preferred sources. This avoids accidental double-counting of superseded rulebooks. citeturn23view3turn26view2turn28search0

A small number of optional public-web sources were seen but not retained as preferred rows because current official provenance or general applicability was weaker than the preferred source set. The clearest examples are older or narrowly scoped competition documents and generic institution pages that did not add distinct evaluative value beyond the retained source family. This is a normalisation choice, not an unresolved mandatory-source gap.

## Early Evidence-Gap Watchlist

The most important watchpoint for extraction is the gap between **strong ballet/contemporary admissions evidence** and **thinner formal public criteria for jazz, tap, commercial/street and hip-hop**. Those latter styles are represented, but more often via competition rules, mixed vocational programmes or practitioner guidance than via standalone conservatoire rubrics.

A second watchpoint is **tape-observable versus live-room-only evidence**. Several sources make it clear that schools and companies use workshops, interviews, improvisation, callbacks or class learning to assess things that a static self-tape may not fully show. Later extraction must separate what can genuinely be inferred from a recorded dance submission from what belongs to a live audition.

A third watchpoint is **full-body visibility, safe space and assessability**. A useful source cluster exists around London Studio Centre, USC Kaufman, Arden, Mountview, GSA and One Dance UK safe-space guidance, but these will need disciplined extraction so that later rubric design values assessability rather than expensive production polish.

A fourth watchpoint is **accessibility-safe physicality**. Equity, Candoco, One Dance UK, RAD and ISTD all point toward access and adjustment principles, but later work must be careful not to translate these into inappropriate assumptions about capacity, stamina, flexibility or “correct” physical presentation from tape alone.

A fifth watchpoint is **category leakage**, especially the current risk that dance-only tapes inherit “vocal” or theatre-style language. The census confirms this as an audit target, but the census itself does not solve it.

A final watchpoint is **choreography pickup / learning speed**. This clearly matters in live schools/company environments, yet the public-web evidence found so far often treats it as workshop or callback behaviour. Later extraction should test whether enough tape-based evidence exists to say anything reliable beyond what is explicitly shown in the recorded task. citeturn18search0turn13search0turn27search5turn17search2turn17search9

## Reusable Handoff Pack for DANCE-B1

### Handoff summary

DANCE-S0 is complete and the Dance branch is ready to move into **DANCE-B1 extraction** using the same disciplined workflow established in the Musical Theatre pilot: source-led extraction first, then synthesis, then gap audit and revision. The B1 batch is intentionally large because official admissions and conservatoire sources are the strongest public evidence for what dance programmes actually ask applicants to demonstrate, what can be assessed from a recorded submission, and how schools distinguish present readiness from training potential.

The B1 ledger is strongest in ballet and contemporary admissions, with good additional coverage for mixed vocational pathways, commercial dance and musical-theatre-adjacent dance routes. Several schools provide explicit video or filmed-audition guidance, which is important because the current TapeCoach baseline has known dance assessability risks around full-body visibility, camera distance, safe space and over-rewarding production polish. B1 also contains several admissions-policy or audition-pack PDFs that are likely to yield higher-confidence extraction than general marketing pages, especially for selection criteria, access provisions, reasonable adjustments and process boundaries.

Important normalisation points for B1: Urdang has multiple public domains, so use the dedicated Urdang admissions pages as preferred current sources; Royal Ballet School and ENBS each have both overview pages and more detailed current-cycle pages or packs, so extract from the detailed current-cycle source first; The Place/LCDS has parallel study and course pages, both worth using because the course pages add workshop and interview specifics. Video-application pages embedded inside admissions processes, such as Central, London Studio Centre and USC Kaufman, remain B1 sources because they are part of official selection requirements, not merely generic filming advice.

When extracting B1, prioritise: explicit audition tasks, technique classes requested, solo requirements, improvisation/interview/workshop elements, what schools say they assess, what they say about potential versus current level, what is observable from a video submission, and any accessibility or support language attached directly to the admissions process.

### B1 alias / duplicate notes

The preferred **Urdang** admissions source is `urdang.citystgeorges.ac.uk/how-to-apply`; `theurdang.london` and City-hosted course pages are supporting aliases or companion pages, not separate duplicate institutions. The preferred **Royal Ballet School** source is the current UK-auditions page, rather than the broader auditions landing page. The preferred **ENBS** detailed source is the 2026 audition pack, paired with the Senior School Auditions page. The preferred **The Place / LCDS** extraction path should begin with the course pages because they contain more concrete workshop and interview detail than the broader study page. Video-guidance pages embedded inside official admissions processes remain B1 rather than B4 because they are part of the school’s current selection route. citeturn6search0turn6search4turn1search4turn23view2turn2search14

## Audit readiness and inputs

### Audit readiness check

- **Current Dance baseline materials present:** **Yes**
- **Completed DANCE-SYN handoff present:** **Yes**
- **Example Dance outputs present:** **No**
- **Source IDs normalised:** **Yes**
- **Audit may proceed:** **Yes**

**Caveats**

The baseline pack is sufficient for a full wording-and-guidance audit, but not for a full implementation audit. The strongest baseline materials for this audit are:

- **Primary baseline materials:** prompt **0B** (Dance rubric slice), prompt **0E** (Baseline Guardrail Pack), attachment **0C — Current Process and Rubric Baseline Audit**, attachment **0D — Current Output Specificity Stress Test**
- **Supporting baseline materials:** attachment **0A-RECONCILE — Rubric Design Memory vs Current Implementation**, attachment **0 — GPT Rubric Control Sheet**

That means the attachments that should be treated as **baseline materials** are **0C and 0D as primary attachments**, with **0A** and **0 — GPT Rubric Control Sheet** used as supporting control/context documents. Prompt sections **0B** and **0E** remain binding because they are the most explicit Dance-specific baseline inputs.

What was **not** supplied:
- current frontend label-helper code
- current comparison-page label-helper code
- actual current Dance report examples
- raw current Dance prompt text beyond the supplied baseline slices
- current renderer/export behaviour for Dance specifically

So this audit can assess **baseline wording, logic framing, guardrails and report-structure intent**, but cannot fully certify live UI behaviour.

### Audit scope and out-of-scope

**This audit covers**
- conflicts between the current Dance baseline and DANCE-SYN findings
- missing or underspecified dance wording and report guidance
- user-facing label risk within the existing six-field model
- evidence-anchor requirements
- style-specific versus generic movement language
- tape-observable versus live-room-only boundaries
- anti-bias and accessibility-safe language
- production-value versus assessability boundaries
- revision targets for DANCE-REV
- provisional non-regression tests

**This audit does not cover**
- backend logic changes
- schema changes
- score-field additions
- score-field renames in code
- weight changes
- cap or blocker changes
- verdict-threshold changes
- Mux or pipeline changes
- implementation of subtype extraction
- UI implementation beyond audit notes on wording, suppression and guardrails

**Intentionally deferred to DANCE-REV**
- actual revised sentence-level wording
- exact user-facing section text
- finalised label wording
- finalised confidence caveat wording
- finalised anti-bias rule wording
- finalised timestamp wording and report phrasing

**Out of scope because of architecture guardrails**
- replacing the stored `vocal` field
- altering the shared six-field score architecture
- adding a true dedicated dance-technique score field
- changing server-side recomputation
- changing public report schema or comparison-page data structures

## Topic summary and safeguard audit

### Topic-by-topic audit summary

**Style-specific movement technique language**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: one generic movement-technique bucket, plus the `vocal` proxy, encourages interchangeable feedback across ballet, contemporary, jazz, tap, commercial and street forms.  
Recommendation IDs: **R01, R02, R13**.  
Revision scope note: revise movement-technique guidance, style-specific guidance blocks and dance-only label handling.

**Technical / video assessability**  
Current baseline status: **Partial**.  
Key risk: visibility and assessability are recognised, but not formalised as dance-specific preconditions.  
Recommendation IDs: **R03, R14**.  
Revision scope note: revise tape assessability guidance, technical/video guidance and reliability wording.

**Audio / music assessability**  
Current baseline status: **Partial**.  
Key risk: weak or unclear soundtrack can be mistaken for weak musicality or poor tap/rhythm quality.  
Recommendation IDs: **R03, R11, R12**.  
Revision scope note: revise audio/music assessability guidance and reliability language.

**Acting / performance / artistry overlap**  
Current baseline status: **Partial**.  
Key risk: shared acting-field language can produce theatre-style or vague “presence” language rather than movement-based expression.  
Recommendation IDs: **R13**.  
Revision scope note: revise performance/artistry guidance and category breakdown wording.

**professional_presentation boundaries**  
Current baseline status: **Partial**.  
Key risk: polish, glamour, equipment quality or “professional look” can leak into dance judgement.  
Recommendation IDs: **R07**.  
Revision scope note: revise professional_presentation guidance and presentation-note rules.

**Dance-only label risk**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: dance-only reports may display singing-coded language because of the stored `vocal` proxy.  
Recommendation IDs: **R01**.  
Revision scope note: revise dance-only output display / label handling note.

**Current vocal-proxy risk**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: the field meaning changes across singing, speech and movement technique, which is confusing for users and destabilises category interpretation.  
Recommendation IDs: **R01, R02**.  
Revision scope note: contain via wording and label handling; do not alter architecture in this run.

**Live-room-only versus tape-observable claims**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: pickup speed, response to direction, adaptability, interview readiness and long-day stamina may be overclaimed from finished tape.  
Recommendation IDs: **R05**.  
Revision scope note: add live-room-only caveat language and claim-scope rules.

**Accessibility-safe assessment**  
Current baseline status: **Partial**.  
Key risk: access needs may still be framed as performance deficits if process-adaptation language is not made explicit.  
Recommendation IDs: **R06**.  
Revision scope note: strengthen exclusion / anti-bias rules and accessibility-safe assessment language.

**Generic feedback suppression**  
Current baseline status: **Partial**.  
Key risk: broad praise such as “good musicality” or “strong performance” can still slip through without movement or timing evidence.  
Recommendation IDs: **R04, R14**.  
Revision scope note: strengthen evidence-anchor rules across headline, category notes, strengths, improvements and timestamps.

**Production-value versus assessability**  
Current baseline status: **Partial**.  
Key risk: polished tapes can be over-rewarded and simple, home-shot but readable tapes can be undervalued.  
Recommendation IDs: **R03, R07**.  
Revision scope note: tighten presentation, assessability and reliability rules.

**Choreography pick-up / learning-speed caution**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: finished tape may be treated as evidence of quick learning or direction response when those are usually live-room tests.  
Recommendation IDs: **R05**.  
Revision scope note: add explicit live-room-only claim boundaries.

**Stamina / endurance caution**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: short clips can invite unsupported claims about endurance, fatigue handling or full-call reliability.  
Recommendation IDs: **R05**.  
Revision scope note: add explicit anti-overclaim language in live-only caveats.

**Commercial / street / hip-hop caution**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: employer- and competition-shaped criteria may be written as universal commercial-dance standards.  
Recommendation IDs: **R10**.  
Revision scope note: add style-specific caution language and limitation wording.

**Tap evidence limits**  
Current baseline status: **Non-compliant**.  
Key risk: strong tap comments may be made where rhythmic audibility is not actually reliable.  
Recommendation IDs: **R11, R12**.  
Revision scope note: add tap-specific guidance and audio/music caveats.

## Reusable handoff pack for DANCE-REV

### DANCE-AUDIT handoff summary

The Dance audit is complete and the baseline is now clearly mapped against the completed Dance synthesis. The strongest audit conclusion is that the current Dance baseline is **not wrongly directed**, but it is still **too generic, too shared-schema-shaped, and too weakly bounded** for evidence-led Dance reporting unless it is revised before rollout. The two biggest structural pressures are already acknowledged by the baseline itself: first, Dance still relies on the shared six-field architecture; second, the current `vocal` field is still being used as a movement-technique proxy, which creates immediate user-facing label risk in dance-only situations. That issue is real, but it is also partly architectural, so DANCE-REV should address it first through wording, user-facing label handling and exclusion rules rather than through schema change.

The highest-priority content issue is **style specificity**. The synthesis supports different evidence vocabularies for ballet, contemporary, jazz/modern theatre, tap, commercial, street/hip-hop and MT dance, while the current baseline still operates largely through a generic movement bucket. The second high-priority issue is **assessability**. Full-body visibility, stable framing, readable space, audible music and low-edit setup are not aesthetic preferences; they are preconditions for fair dance judgement from tape. The baseline currently gestures towards that, but does not yet codify it strongly enough.

The third high-priority issue is **claim scope**. The current baseline does not yet ring-fence live-room-only capacities tightly enough. Choreography pick-up, response to direction, adaptability, workshop behaviour and long-day stamina should be treated as live-room or callback evidence unless directly shown. The fourth is **accessibility-safe assessment**. Existing anti-penalisation language is useful, but DANCE-REV must separate process adaptation from attainment much more explicitly and block capability, medical-history and access-need inference.

None of the remaining issues block DANCE-REV. The most important limitations to carry forward are: the structural vocal-proxy risk, universal commercial/street/hip-hop descriptor limits, tap limits outside exam-board evidence, and the absence of actual current Dance report examples for spot-auditing.

**Final Audit Scope and Preservation Rules**

This final audit covers acceptance of the revised Dance wording, guardrails, addenda and traceability against the completed Dance synthesis and Dance audit. It tests whether the revision package materially answers the audited problems without destabilising the preserved shared system. It does not test live implementation behaviour, frontend label rendering, comparison-page category labelling, rendered/exported Dance reports, or real output execution, because those materials were not supplied in this run.

The following remain out of scope because of explicit architecture and implementation guardrails: backend logic, schema, score-field architecture, weights, caps, blockers, verdict thresholds, role-fit bounds, server-side recomputation, Mux or pipeline flow, Step 1 / Step 2 process shape, and the stabilised Musical Theatre acting-plus-song flow. Those constraints are explicitly preserved by the control materials and by the revision package itself. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file3

A return to DANCE-REV would be required only if this audit found that the revision package failed materially on one of the core high-priority audit targets: dance-only label containment, style-specific Dance language, tape assessability preconditions, live-room-only claim boundaries, accessibility-safe assessment, or protection of the shared-system / Musical Theatre non-regression envelope. On the supplied materials, that threshold is not met.

## Acceptance Review

The revised package is materially responsive to the audit. It closes the most important wording and guardrail gaps that the control files had already exposed: the dance-only label hazard created by the overloaded `vocal` field, the lack of explicit assessability preconditions, generic unsupported Dance praise, live-room overclaim, loose professional-presentation logic, and insufficiently explicit accessibility-safe adaptation language. The control files independently support why those were the correct revision targets. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file3

## Final Release Decision and Handoff

**Final Release Decision**

**DANCE-FINAL-D01 — Approved with explicit limitations**

The revised Dance baseline is materially compliant with the completed synthesis and materially responsive to the completed audit at wording-and-guardrail level. It now contains the dance-only vocal-proxy risk as far as the current architecture allows, introduces style-aware Dance handling, makes assessability a genuine precondition, blocks generic unsupported praise, ring-fences live-room-only capacities, strengthens accessibility-safe assessment, tightens professional-presentation boundaries, and adds a Dance-specific timestamp / reliability rule-set. None of the preserved shared-system constraints or Musical Theatre non-regression constraints are destabilised by the revision.

There are no critical blockers in the revised text that require a forced return to DANCE-REV before the next stage. The remaining issues are limitations, not release blockers at baseline-text level: partly structural vocal-proxy semantics, unverified frontend label-helper behaviour, unverified comparison-page label behaviour, unverified renderer/export note behaviour, limited commercial/street/hip-hop universality, thinner tap evidence outside formal frameworks, and the absence of live Dance report examples for spot-auditing.

**DANCE-FINAL-D02 — Approved for Output Specificity / Non-Regression Test Mapping with explicit limitation set**

The next stage can move forward on the basis of the accepted revision package. What must move forward explicitly are the test clusters around display-layer label containment, assessability preconditions, anti-polish boundaries, evidence-anchor enforcement, live-room-only overclaim suppression, accessibility-safe output language, commercial/street caution, tap audibility, and timestamp rendering / density. What must remain openly listed as limitations are DANCE-FINAL-I01 to DANCE-FINAL-I08.

**Reusable Handoff Pack for the Next Stage**

**DANCE-FINAL-AUDIT handoff summary**

The final audit confirms that the Dance revision package is materially fit for the next stage. The revised baseline now answers the highest-risk Dance problems at wording-and-guardrail level without disturbing the shared architecture that the control materials require TapeCoach to preserve. Most importantly, it contains the dance-only vocal-proxy problem in user-facing language, adds style-specific Dance handling inside the existing shared framework, and codifies assessability preconditions so that full-body or task-sufficient visibility, stable framing, readable space, audible music where relevant, continuity and simple capture are treated as fairness conditions, not aesthetic preferences.

The revised baseline also now makes clear that Dance reports must be evidence-led. Generic phrases such as good energy, strong technique, nice movement or strong performance are no longer acceptable unless they are anchored to visible movement, a task, a timestamp, a style-specific feature, or an assessability condition. Live-room-only capacities are also materially better protected: choreography pick-up, response to direction, adaptability, workshop behaviour and stamina are now marked as mainly live-room or callback evidence unless directly shown.

Accessibility-safe assessment is materially improved. The revised baseline now separates process adaptation from attainment and blocks deficit inference from mobility aids, seated adaptation, reduced range, convalescence, bespoke pathways or body difference. professional_presentation is also properly constrained: it now covers assessability, brief response and safe preparation, not glamour, polish, physique or expensive production.

The remaining risks are real but non-blocking. They are mostly the same as the ones already flagged in the audit and revision handoffs: the structural vocal-proxy issue remains partly architectural; commercial/street/hip-hop descriptors are less universal than ballet/contemporary/jazz/tap; tap remains thinner outside formal frameworks; and actual Dance report rendering, label-helper behaviour and output specificity were not directly auditable from the supplied materials. Those issues should now be handled through output-specificity and non-regression testing rather than another wording loop.

## Dance output specificity standard

The standard below translates the accepted revision into concrete user-facing requirements. It is intentionally strict about three things that the baseline-control materials show to be fragile today: label semantics, evidence anchoring, and note density. It also preserves the shared-system constraint that nothing in this mapping may imply a backend field, schema or scoring change. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1 fileciteturn0file2

| Casting insight / readiness summary | Submission-readiness summary grounded in present-tape evidence | Observable level, assessability condition and scope boundary | Link readiness to the actual style/task being shown | Use cautious readiness language without guessing subtype | Strong potential for industry work in generic employer context | R03, R05, R08 | S03/C03, S08/C05, S09/C08 | F03, F05, F07, F13 |
| Category breakdown | Each visible category note must reflect what the category means in Dance | One category-specific observation per visible category | Technique note must use style-appropriate domains | Use shared movement domains only | Static vocal-language leakage; generic acting-language leakage | R01, R02, R04, R12, R13 | S01/C01, S02/C02, S11/C04, S04/C12, S05/C13 | F01, F02, F04, F12, F14 |

| Musicality / rhythm note | Separate the performer’s rhythmic relationship from audibility problems | Audible music or visible count/phrase relationship | Use style-relevant rhythm language; tap requires audible footwork | State that musical judgement is limited if sound/style evidence is weak | Weak musicality because soundtrack is faint | R11, R12 | S04/C11, S04/C12 | F03, F11 |
| Technical / assessability note | Describe whether the tape is judgeable, not whether it is polished | Full-body/task visibility, framing, space, continuity, safety | Mention any style/task visibility need, such as floorwork or line | State which shared movement evidence was and was not readable | Professional setup with no assessability consequence | R03, R07 | S03/C03, S06/C07 | F03, F09, F12 |

| Feedback reliability note | Reflect assessability limits openly | Visibility, sound, framing, continuity and task scope | Style does not change reliability logic; assessability does | Explicitly mark style confidence low if style is unclear | High reliability where body or music is unreadable | R03, R12, R14 | S03/C03, S04/C12, S12/C14 | F03, F11, F13 |

**Style-Specific Dance Output Rules**

| Style / context | Observable technical domains that may be named | Observable performance / communication domains that may be named | Extra assessability requirement, if any | Caution language required | What must not be overclaimed | Example acceptable phrasing pattern | Example blocked phrasing pattern | Related DANCE-REV section / change ID(s) | Related DANCE-SYN finding ID(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ballet | Placement, posture, line, coordination, control, timing, spatial clarity | Projection through line, phrasing, musical responsiveness, stylistic precision | Enough distance/body visibility to read line and placement | If placement or full line is partly cropped, say so | Universal “classical quality” without observable support | “The adage phrase from 00:18–00:31 reads with clear placement and line, though the turn exit softens the finish.” | “Beautiful classical quality throughout.” | S02/C02, S03/C03, S11/C04 | F02, F03, F14 |
| Contemporary / modern | Weight, alignment, breath, flow, coordination, use of space, dynamic range | Intent through phrasing, focus, spatial intention, dynamic contrast | Enough space/body visibility to read floorwork or travelling pathways | Creative language only if the task visibly includes open material or improvisation | General “very creative” from fixed phrase alone | “At 00:42 the weight shift into the floor phrase reads clearly through breath and directional change.” | “Very creative and expressive throughout.” | S02/C02, S03/C03, S09/C09 | F02, F03, F06, F14 |
| Jazz / modern theatre | Precision, line, attack/release, rhythm/timing, projection, use of space | Performance energy through accents, phrase finish, style/theme clarity | Full-body readability for directional changes and line | Keep “performance” movement-based, not theatre-acting-based | Generic “star quality” or “great acting” | “The syncopated phrase at 00:25 lands cleanly with clear attack and musical fit.” | “Great performer with lots of star quality.” | S02/C02, S05/C13, S11/C04 | F02, F04, F14 |
| Tap | Precision of footwork, rhythmic interpretation, attack, phrase control | Communication through rhythmic clarity and phrasing | Relevant footwork sound must be audible | If sound is weak, rhythm judgement must be limited explicitly | Strong rhythmic-clarity claims without audible evidence | “The time-step pattern is visible, but the recording does not make the footwork sound clear enough for a strong rhythmic-clarity judgement.” | “Your tap sounds clean and precise,” where the sound is unreadable | S04/C11, S04/C12, S11/C04 | F03, F11 |
| Commercial dance | Phrasing, coordination, groove, attack/release, camera readability where relevant | Style fit, clarity of hook phrase, musical fit, movement-based confidence | If camera relationship matters, the frame must still show the movement clearly | Employer-specific expectations must stay contextual, not universal | Bookability, look, marketability as dance merit | “The hook phrase reads clearly on camera and the accents stay consistent through the chorus.” | “You look highly bookable for commercial work.” | S02/C02, S06/C07, S10/C10 | F10, F12, F14 |
| Street / hip-hop | Groove, whole-body clarity, coordination, phrasing, style coherence where reasonably inferable | Musical fit, attack/release, movement clarity through groove | Whole-body visibility matters for groove and foot-floor relation | Cultural/universal authenticity claims must be cautious and evidence-led | Universal “authentic hip-hop” claim from mixed or unclear tape | “The groove stays readable through torso and feet at 00:36–00:48, though the style mix reads more commercial-street than one codified form.” | “This is authentic hip-hop technique,” without a stronger basis | S02/C02, S10/C10, S11/C04 | F10, F14 |
| MT dance | Movement clarity, timing, line where relevant, choreographic communication, musical responsiveness | Intention through movement, relation to song structure, phrase finish | Enough full-body/task visibility to relate movement to musical material | Avoid turning it into spoken acting analysis unless spoken acting exists | Character-acting claims not shown through movement | “The phrase communicates musical intention through clear accents and directional changes into the chorus.” | “Great acting choices throughout the dance phrase.” | S02/C02, S05/C13, S11/C04 | F02, F04, F14 |
| Mixed / uncertain style | Shared domains only: control, timing, coordination, clarity, use of space, transitions | Movement-based communication only where visible | Assessability must still be strong enough for the shared domains | State mixed/uncertain style directly | Forced subtype certainty | “The tape shows clear timing and transitions, but the style reads as a mixed commercial/contemporary blend rather than one single codified form.” | “This is definitely jazz,” without adequate support | S02/C02, S03/C03 | F03, F14 |
| Dance tape with no style inferable | Shared movement domains only | Movement-based communication only | No extra style requirement beyond readable movement | Say style cannot be named confidently | Any invented style label | “Movement clarity and timing are assessable, but the tape does not supply enough style information for a tighter label.” | “Strong contemporary quality,” without evidence | S02/C02, S03/C03 | F03, F14 |
| Inclusive / adapted dance context overlay | Judge phrasing, timing, clarity, coordination, spatial intention, task communication as shown | Communication through adapted phrasing, focus, dynamics and task clarity | Assessability must be judged relative to the shown adaptation, not a default body norm | Adaptation must be described without deficit inference | Despite the chair; limited because of mobility aid; lower potential because adapted | “The seated adaptation communicates the rhythm and directional intent clearly through the phrase at 00:21–00:34.” | “Impressive despite the chair.” | S07/C06, S11/C04 | F08 |

**Generic-Feedback Suppression Map**

| Generic phrase | Why it is too generic | What evidence would be required | Example acceptable replacement pattern | Example blocked pattern | Related DANCE-OS rule ID(s) | Related DANCE-REV change ID(s) | Related DANCE-SYN finding ID(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| good energy | Says nothing about where or how the movement reads | Phrase, dynamic change, attack/release or travel moment | “From 00:34 the second travelling phrase gains sharper attack and rebound, which lifts the section’s momentum.” | “Good energy throughout.” | R04, R13 | C04, C13 | F04 |
| nice movement | Transferable to almost any tape | What movement, where, why it reads clearly | “At 00:18 the turn preparation and exit are clearly readable, which makes the phrase land cleanly.” | “Nice movement.” | R04 | C04 | F04 |
| strong performance | Too broad and often acting-shaped | Movement-based communication evidence | “The phrase communicates intention through the held focus and dynamic contrast into the final accent.” | “Strong performance overall.” | R04, R13 | C04, C13 | F04, F14 |
| good control | Missing domain and moment | Specific placement, timing, balance, transition or finish | “The landing from the jump phrase remains controlled through the next transition at 00:41.” | “Good control.” | R04 | C04 | F04 |
| strong technique | Empty unless tied to visible domains | Technical domain + style/task + moment | “The jazz phrase shows clean timing and line through the kick-ball-change sequence at 00:27.” | “Strong technique.” | R02, R04 | C02, C04 | F02, F14 |
| good musicality | Can confuse audibility with judgement | Audible music relation, count relation or visible phrasing | “At 00:30 the phrase lands neatly with the musical accents, especially through the held pause before the turn.” | “Good musicality.” | R11, R12, R04 | C11, C12, C04 | F03, F11 |
| great presence | Generic and often look-biased | Visible focus, projection or phrase command | “The centre phrase holds attention because the focus stays clear and the dynamics stay consistent through the final eight counts.” | “Great presence.” | R04, R13, R07 | C04, C13, C07 | F04, F12 |
| expressive | Too vague without movement evidence | Dynamics, phrasing, focus, spatial intention | “The softer release into the floor phrase at 00:46 gives the section a clear dynamic shift.” | “Very expressive.” | R04, R13 | C04, C13 | F04 |
| clear style | Needs a named style indicator | Style cue, phrasing cue, attack, groove or line | “The groove and torso-led phrasing make the commercial-street blend readable from 00:36 onward.” | “Clear style.” | R02, R10, R04 | C02, C10, C04 | F10, F14 |
| good rhythm | Too unspecific and can ignore sound issues | Visible phrasing or audible count relation | “The footwork stays aligned to the count through the second phrase, although the track is too low for a stronger rhythmic claim.” | “Good rhythm.” | R11, R12, R04 | C11, C12, C04 | F03, F11 |

| confident performer | Easily becomes generic or appearance-based | Visible attack, commitment to phrase or sustained focus | “The opening phrase commits clearly to the accents and directional changes, which makes the start read decisively.” | “Confident performer.” | R04, R13 | C04, C13 | F04 |

## Concrete test mapping and adversarial scenarios

The next-stage QA burden should focus on whether outputs actually honour the revised wording under adversarial conditions. The control materials already show where similar failures have surfaced in other disciplines: static labels, thin timestamps, generic praise, overconfident brief adherence, and uncertainty about what the UI or export layer actually renders. fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

**Concrete Test Map from Preserved Test Clusters**

| Test ID or cluster | Concrete scenario | What inputs/conditions the scenario assumes | What the output must do | What the output must not do | Must-have evidence anchors | Must-have caveat / limitation wording | Style-specificity requirement | Reliability / confidence effect | Related DANCE-OS test ID(s) | Related DANCE-REV change / section ID(s) | Final pass / fail criteria |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T01–T04 | Cropped or partial-body Dance tape | Dance-only tape; lower legs or full line not consistently visible | Describe assessability limit first; narrow technical claims | Strong line/footwork claims from what cannot be seen | Cropping fact; affected phrase or body area | “This limits how confidently line/footwork can be judged.” | Use shared domains only if subtype cannot be supported | Lower reliability if material limitation is meaningful | DANCE-OS-T04 | C03/S03, C04/S11, C14/S12 | Pass if output names the visibility limit and avoids overclaim |
| T01–T04 | Music weak or partly inaudible, but movement visible | Dance tape with audible visual timing but weak soundtrack | Separate sound-readability from movement judgement | Convert poor sound into poor musicality by default | Sound condition; what remains visible | “The soundtrack is too weak for a stronger musicality claim.” | Tap-specific caveat if tap; otherwise visible phrasing only | Lower confidence for rhythm/music comments | DANCE-OS-T05 | C11/S04, C12/S04, C03/S03 | Pass if output preserves movement judgement but narrows rhythmic certainty |
| T01–T04 | Smartphone/home setup that is still assessable | Dance-only tape filmed simply at home; movement readable | Accept simple capture if the phrase is readable | Penalise domestic setting or lack of polish | Stable frame, readable space, continuity | “Simple capture is acceptable because the movement remains readable.” | Name style only if visible | Reliability may remain high if assessability is good | DANCE-OS-T02 | C03/S03, C07/S06 | Pass if no polish bias appears |
| T01–T04 | High production polish with weak assessability | Professionally lit/stylised tape, but crop/edit/space hinders judgement | Prioritise assessability over polish | Reward studio look as dance merit | Specific unreadability fact | “Production quality does not offset the assessability limit.” | Style mention secondary to assessability | Lower reliability if movement remains hard to judge | DANCE-OS-T03 | C03/S03, C07/S06 | Pass if polish is neutralised and limitation is foregrounded |
| T05 | Dance-only tape with no singing present | Pure dance tape; no spoken or sung vocal content | Hide or reinterpret vocal semantics as Dance technique | Show voice/singing category language | Dance-only absence of singing | “This category reflects movement technique, not singing.” where relevant | Style-specific if known; shared domains if not | None by itself unless other assessability issues exist | DANCE-OS-T01 | C01/S01 | Pass if no voice/singing wording appears anywhere user-facing |
| T06–T07 | Mixed-style tape with unclear subtype | Dance tape shows commercial/street blend or unclear style | Use mixed/uncertain style fallback and evidence anchors | Force a single subtype with unjustified certainty | Observable groove/phrasing/coordination cue | “The style reads as mixed/uncertain rather than one codified form.” | Must avoid universal claims | Reliability can stay high if movement is readable, but style confidence must be narrower | DANCE-OS-T08, T15 | C02/S02, C10/S10, C04/S11 | Pass if wording stays specific but cautious |
| T06–T07 | Contemporary tape with visible improvisation task | Tape or brief explicitly includes improvisation/open task | Permit creative/improvisational language, but tie it to the task | Use generic “creative” praise without task evidence | Timestamped open-task moment | “Because the task includes improvisation...” | Use contemporary/open-task vocabulary | Reliability depends on assessability, not solely on task type | DANCE-OS-T09 | C09/S09, C02/S02, C04/S11 | Pass if creativity is grounded in the actual task |
| T08–T10 | Finished polished tape where pick-up and direction response are unknown | Reel-style or first-round tape; no learning/redirection visible | Mark those capacities not assessable or low-confidence | Infer quick learning or responsiveness from polish alone | Absence of learning/redirection evidence | “Pick-up speed and response to direction are not assessable from this finished tape alone.” | None beyond actual style note | Confidence narrowed for those capacities only | DANCE-OS-T11 | C05/S08 | Pass if output blocks live-room overclaim |
| T08–T10 | Short clip where stamina is unknown | Short dance clip with no long-call evidence | Keep stamina out of positive/negative claims | Infer endurance from a short excerpt | Clip length and task limit | “Stamina across a longer call cannot be judged from this short clip alone.” | None | Confidence narrowed for stamina specifically | DANCE-OS-T12 | C05/S08 | Pass if stamina is explicitly ring-fenced |
| T08–T10 | Visible mobility aid or seated adaptation | Adapted dance tape with clear mobility aid/seated choreography | Judge only task clarity and shown movement | Treat adaptation as deficit or inspirational exception | Visible adaptation and actual movement evidence | “The adaptation is part of how the task is communicated, not a deficit.” | Use style overlay if style identifiable | Reliability should not drop merely because of adaptation | DANCE-OS-T07 | C06/S07 | Pass if no deficit inference appears |
| T11–T13 | Mixed commercial/street tape | Employer-shaped or mixed-style commercial/street reel | Describe groove, phrasing and style coherence cautiously | Universalise employer or competition logic | Observable style blend cue | “The tape reads as a commercial/street blend rather than a universal benchmark for one form.” | Must name blend or uncertainty if needed | Reliability depends on readability, not universality | DANCE-OS-T08 | C10/S10, C02/S02 | Pass if wording stays contextual and tape-specific |

**Output-Specificity Decision**

**DANCE-OS-D01 — Approved with explicit limitations**

The approved revision package is strong enough to be translated into a concrete Dance output-specificity standard. The resulting standard is materially aligned with the accepted final-audit position: it preserves the shared architecture, contains the dance-only vocal-proxy risk at wording level, makes assessability a genuine precondition, blocks unsupported generic praise, separates audio/music readability from musicality, constrains professional-presentation language, protects inclusive/adapted contexts, and ring-fences live-room-only capacities.

**DANCE-OS-D02 — Approved for live Dance output QA / regression execution**

Live Dance output QA and regression execution can move forward immediately on the basis of this mapping. The next-stage priority is not another wording rewrite, but live verification of label containment, comparison-page naming, timestamp rendering, reliability fallback, anti-polish boundaries, anti-bias compliance, commercial/street caution, and tap audibility handling. Live-output examples are still needed before release sign-off, but their absence does not block this mapping stage.

## Reusable handoff and completion

**DANCE-OUTPUT-SPEC handoff summary**

The Dance output-specificity mapping is complete and the revised baseline is now translated into a concrete QA-ready standard. The strongest result is that the revised Dance rules can now be tested as output behaviour rather than treated as abstract rubric wording. In practical terms, Dance outputs must now behave as if assessability comes first. Full-body or task-sufficient visibility, stable framing, readable space, audible music where relevant, continuity and simple capture are all treated as preconditions for high-confidence comment. Where those conditions do not hold, the output must narrow its claim, state the limitation and reduce reliability instead of substituting generic criticism.

The second major result is that user-facing Dance wording is now tightly bounded. Dance-only outputs must not present the stored vocal slot as singing or voice where singing is absent. Movement technique must be described through style-aware or shared movement domains, not through one generic movement bucket and not through singing language. Performance language is now also constrained: Dance outputs should talk about phrasing, dynamics, focus, spatial intention, musical relation and choreographic communication, not generic acting unless spoken acting genuinely exists.

The third major result is testability. The accepted revision package now maps cleanly into preserved QA clusters: assessability and anti-polish boundaries; dance-only label containment; style specificity and generic-feedback suppression; live-room-only overclaim controls; accessibility-safe wording; commercial/street caution; tap audibility; and context-specific handling of improvisation and training-potential language. Because no live Dance reports were supplied, this handoff remains synthetic and adversarial rather than renderer-verified. That is the main remaining limitation.

Nothing in this mapping destabilises the shared six-field architecture, the two-step pipeline, or the Musical Theatre acting-plus-song anchor. The open issues are therefore limitations to carry into live-output QA, not blockers to the next stage.

## Revision sections and wording

The section package below revises only what is actually present in 0B/0E or adds clearly labelled Dance addenda where the supplied baseline did not yet contain adequate text. The rationale is consistent across the supporting baseline materials: Dance is currently the highest-risk discipline because it lacks a true movement-specific rubric, uses the stored vocal field as a proxy for technique, remains vulnerable to generic wording, and has underdeveloped assessability and timestamp rules. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

**DANCE-REV-S01 — Dance-only category label containment**  
**Baseline source section:** 0B  
**Current baseline excerpt actually being revised:**  
> Operationally, vocal is reused as a movement-technique proxy for dance, which is a known risk.  
> “Vocal” label is misleading unless renamed or hidden.

**Proposed revised text:**  
> In Dance, the stored vocal field may continue to operate internally as the movement-technique slot, but user-facing Dance reports must not present that category as singing, voice or generic vocal performance unless singing is actually present in the tape. In dance-only reports, the user-facing interpretation of that category should be movement technique or dance technique within the current shared framework. Where singing is absent, do not describe the performer as vocally strong or weak.

**Change summary:** Contains the vocal-proxy risk through wording and user-facing interpretation without proposing field or schema change.

## Consolidated revised baseline text

The consolidated package below turns the revision into usable working-draft baseline text. It is driven by the same baseline-side evidence throughout: the current implementation uses a shared schema, Dance still lacks a true dedicated movement rubric, output specificity remains uneven, and timestamp and label risks are real enough to require explicit wording rather than implied good practice alone. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

**Clean Revised Dance Baseline Package**

### A. Revised 0B Dance rubric slice

**Relevant scoring categories**  
Relevant scoring categories remain: technical, audio, vocal, acting, brief_adherence and professional_presentation.  
Operationally, the stored vocal field may continue to function internally as the movement-technique slot for Dance within the current shared architecture. However, user-facing Dance reports must not present that category as singing, voice or generic vocal performance unless singing is actually present in the tape. In dance-only outputs, that category should be interpreted for the user as movement technique or dance technique within the current framework.

**Relevant report sections**  
Relevant Dance report sections remain: category breakdown, professional standards/brief adherence, timestamped notes, fix-first, improvements, technical visibility notes, and presentation only where camera readability or setup materially affects assessability.  
Dance reports should also use strengths, improvements, fix-first and timestamps to show what was actually observable in this performer, in this tape, in this choreography/task, and in this dance style where known.

**Current discipline logic**  
Dance is supported as an audition type inside the existing shared framework. The system should assess only what is observable in the recorded submission. Valid Dance evidence includes visible movement execution, control, coordination, rhythm/timing, musical responsiveness, use of space, clarity of phrase, transitions, style indicators where identifiable, and movement-based expression/communication.  
The report must clearly separate tape-observable evidence from live-room-only or callback-only capacities. Choreography pick-up speed, response to direction, adaptability after feedback, group-room behaviour, interview readiness and long-day stamina should not be treated as strongly assessable from a finished dance tape unless the tape itself directly shows them.

**Feedback specificity rules**  
Dance feedback must be style-aware wherever the brief, task or tape makes the style reasonably identifiable. Use the most specific supported label available: ballet, contemporary/modern, jazz/modern theatre, tap, commercial dance, street/hip-hop, or MT dance. If style is mixed or unclear, say so and keep wording to shared observable domains rather than guessing.  
Generic praise or criticism is not sufficient. Terms such as good energy, nice movement, strong performance, good control, strong technique, good musicality, great presence, expressive, clear style, good rhythm, professional tape, confident performer, clean lines and good dynamics must be replaced with observable evidence, a named task or phrase, a timestamp, a style-specific attribute, or a clear assessability condition.

**Dance tape assessability**  
Strong Dance judgement from tape depends on assessability first. High-confidence Dance feedback requires enough body and space to read the relevant movement, stable framing, readable movement continuity, audible music where musical judgement depends on it, and a simple enough capture to show what the performer is actually doing. If those conditions are partly missing, the report must narrow claim scope, state the limitation, and lower feedback reliability rather than turning the limitation into generic criticism of skill.

**Audio and music assessability**  
Audio in Dance should describe whether the music, counts or relevant rhythmic output are audible enough to support fair movement assessment. It should not be used to imply weak musicality where the rhythmic relationship cannot be heard reliably.  
For tap, do not make strong positive or negative rhythmic-clarity claims unless the relevant footwork sound is sufficiently audible.

**Movement-based expression and communication**  
In Dance, performance language must remain movement-based. Use intention, expression, projection, communication or performance quality only where those ideas are visible through phrasing, dynamics, focus, spatial intention, attack/release, relation to music, or relation to choreographic task. Avoid theatre-acting language unless spoken acting is actually present.

**Professional presentation boundary**  
In Dance, professional_presentation should be limited to assessability, brief response and safe preparation. It may address whether the tape is readable enough to judge, whether stated task requirements were followed, and whether preparation choices supported or hindered safe, fair assessment. It must not reward glamour, physique, expensive production, studio polish, domestic set transformation or employer-specific look rules as general merit. Smartphone or home capture may be fully acceptable if the movement is readable.

**Accessibility-safe assessment**  
Dance assessment must separate process adaptation from attainment. Mobility aids, seated adaptation, reduced range, bespoke training pathway, CV gaps, convalescence, body difference or access need must not be treated as deficits in themselves. Where material is adapted to body or access need, judge only what is shown and how clearly it communicates the task. Do not infer medical history, injury status, capability ceiling or lack of professionalism from appearance, support equipment or visible adaptation.

**Training potential and creative scope**  
Training-potential language should be reserved to admissions-style or training-route contexts where the task and source logic justify it. Elsewhere, the report should prioritise present observable level in this tape.  
Improvisation and creative-response comments may be used only where the task or tape clearly includes improvisation, creative tasking or open material.

**Known gaps / residual architecture note**  
Current baseline limitations remain: the shared six-field architecture is preserved; the stored vocal field still creates a residual structural risk for Dance-only category display; subtype extraction is not fully confirmed as live; commercial/street/hip-hop evidence remains less universally formalised than ballet/contemporary/jazz-adjacent/tap; and actual Dance report rendering is still a final-audit item.

### B. Revised 0E Dance-specific guardrail additions or amendments

**Dance-specific preserve note**  
Preserve the current six stored score fields, weights, caps, blockers, verdict thresholds, server-side recomputation, two-step architecture, safety/material/accessibility scrub layers, report schema, public JSON structure, and the stabilised Musical Theatre acting-plus-song flow. Dance revisions in this pack are wording, evidence-standard and guardrail changes only.

**Dance-specific regression-risk additions**  
Add the following Dance-specific regression risks to the guardrail pack:
- Dance-only report shows “Vocal”, “voice” or singing language where no singing is present.
- Dance report uses one undifferentiated movement label with no style-specific handling and no “style unclear” caution.
- Dance report makes strong judgements where full-body/task-sufficient visibility, readable space or music audibility are materially limited.
- Dance report rewards production polish, studio environment or equipment quality as a proxy for movement quality.
- Dance report infers pick-up speed, direction response, adaptability or stamina from a finished tape alone.
- Dance report treats disability, access need, mobility aid, adaptation, body difference or convalescence as negative evidence.
- Dance report applies commercial/street/hip-hop wording as if it were a universally formalised standard.
- Dance report makes tap rhythm or clarity claims where relevant audibility is insufficient.
- Dance timestamp count or note specificity drops below what an assessable tape should reasonably support.

**Dance-specific specificity guardrails**  
Add the following to the specificity guardrails:
- Every substantive Dance section must anchor claims to observable evidence.
- Category notes must identify the observable basis for the judgement.
- Strengths and improvements must not rely on generic praise terms alone.
- Fix-first must identify the highest-impact observable change.
- Timestamped notes must be chronological, evidence-led and tied to style/task or assessability.
- If style is unknown, mixed or only partly inferable, mark that cautiously rather than guessing.
- If assessability is materially limited, narrow claim scope and lower reliability rather than padding the report with generic wording.

**Dance-specific scoring and presentation guardrails**  
Add the following to the scoring guardrails:
- Do not present the Dance technique proxy as singing or voice where singing is absent.
- Do not show user-facing singing/voice language in dance-only situations unless singing is actually present.
- Do not score unsupported live-room capacities from a finished Dance tape.
- Do not infer weak musicality from poor music audibility alone.
- Do not reward expensive production, studio polish, employer-specific “look”, glamour or physique as general Dance merit.
- Do not allow presentation notes to drift beyond assessability, brief response or safe preparation.
- Do not let technical/presentation categories dominate unless assessability or explicit brief compliance is materially affected.

### C. New Dance addenda where no adequate baseline text existed

**Dance addendum: style-specific guidance blocks**  
Use the following as style-specific reference language inside the existing framework:
- **Ballet:** placement/posture, line, coordination, control, spatial clarity, musical responsiveness, and style-specific precision where visible.
- **Contemporary / modern:** weight, breath, alignment, flow, use of space, dynamic range, and creative task response where the task includes it.
- **Jazz / modern theatre:** precision, rhythm/timing, projection, line, use of space, style/theme clarity and musical fit.
- **Tap:** precision of footwork, rhythmic interpretation, clarity of attack, audible response where assessable, and overall phrase control.
- **Commercial dance:** clarity of phrasing, groove/style fit, coordination, attack/release, camera readability where relevant, and cautious handling of employer-specific expectations.
- **Street / hip-hop:** groove, phrasing, style authenticity where reasonably inferable, whole-body clarity and musical fit, without presenting competition or employer preferences as universal standards.
- **MT dance:** movement clarity, musical responsiveness, performance intention through movement, style coherence and choreographic communication.

**Dance addendum: live-room-only and low-confidence claim block**  
The following should usually be marked as live-room-only, callback-only or low-confidence unless directly shown: choreography pick-up speed, response to notes, adaptability after direction, stamina across a long call, workshop behaviour, interview readiness and group-room responsiveness. Where such evidence is not directly present, say not assessable or low-confidence.

**Dance addendum: exclusion and anti-bias block**  
Never use the following as positive or negative Dance scoring evidence unless strictly required for safe assessability and directly supported by the task: body type, appearance, height/physique as a universal standard, disability or access need as deficit, injury or medical diagnosis, follower count, fame, social-media behaviour, marketability, bookability, expensive production value, studio polish, cosmetic presentation, generic charisma, stamina claims from short clips, response-to-direction claims from a finished tape, or employer physique rules as a general Dance norm.

## Handoff for final audit

The revision package below is grounded in a now-consistent baseline picture: the current system is stable as a shared-schema self-tape evaluator, but Dance remains the most exposed discipline because technique is still routed through the stored vocal field, subtype handling is underdeveloped, and report specificity depends too heavily on generic shared logic unless it is tightened explicitly. The reconciliation note, control sheet, baseline audit and specificity stress test all point to the same conclusion: the safest path is not a schema rewrite, but a wording-and-guardrail revision that makes Dance more style-specific, more assessability-led, more anti-bias and more resistant to overclaim. fileciteturn0file3 fileciteturn0file2 fileciteturn0file0 fileciteturn0file1

**Reusable Handoff Pack for DANCE-FINAL-AUDIT**

**DANCE-REV handoff summary**

The Dance revision is complete at wording and guardrail level. It does not alter the shared six-field architecture, weights, caps, blockers, verdict thresholds, report schema or backend pipeline. Instead, it makes the Dance baseline materially more specific and more defensible inside the existing system. The most important change is containment of the dance-only vocal-proxy risk. The revision now states plainly that, although the stored vocal field may continue to operate internally as the movement-technique slot, Dance-only reports must not present that category to users as singing or voice unless singing is actually present.

The second major gain is style specificity. The revised baseline now requires style-aware Dance language wherever the brief, task or tape supports it, and it adds explicit handling blocks for ballet, contemporary/modern, jazz/modern theatre, tap, commercial dance, street/hip-hop and MT dance. The third is assessability. Full-body or task-sufficient visibility, stable framing, readable space, audible music where relevant, continuity and simple capture are now codified as preconditions for high-confidence Dance judgement from tape. If those conditions are materially limited, the report must narrow claim scope and lower reliability rather than substituting generic criticism.

The fourth major gain is claim-scope control. Choreography pick-up, direction response, adaptability, workshop behaviour and long-day stamina are now marked as mainly live-room or callback evidence unless directly shown. The fifth is accessibility-safe assessment. The revision makes explicit that process adaptation must be separated from attainment, and that access need, mobility aid, seated adaptation, convalescence, body difference or bespoke pathway must not be treated as negative evidence.

Residual limitations remain, but they do not block final audit: the vocal-proxy issue remains partly structural; commercial/street/hip-hop descriptors remain less universal than ballet/contemporary/jazz/tap; tap remains thinner outside formal frameworks; and actual current Dance report outputs and frontend label behaviour were not supplied for direct spot-auditing.

The principal source-provenance and completeness limitations carried into synthesis are: DANCE-S028 and DANCE-S029 inaccessible; DANCE-S018 and DANCE-S030/S031 partly supported by official page snippets; DANCE-S035 only partly surfaced in its commercial subsection; DANCE-S036 contextual only; DANCE-S040 is a hub rather than a descriptor source; DANCE-S044 is thinner than other ISTD descriptor sources; DANCE-S049 has legacy FAQ formatting; DANCE-S060 was inaccessible; Candoco’s richest source is from 2024 and Stopgap’s strongest extractable notice is from 2022; several employer sources mix strong process/style evidence with company-specific attire, physique or presentation expectations that cannot be generalised.

Overall coverage confidence is **medium-high** for ballet, contemporary, assessability, accessibility and major video-assessment boundaries; **medium** for jazz/modern theatre and commercial dance; **medium-low to medium** for universal street/hip-hop and tap outside exam-board or employer-specific contexts.

## Frameworks and recurring criteria

### Key Dance assessment frameworks found

The completed batches do not produce one single Dance assessment framework. They produce a layered evidence model.

Official school and conservatoire sources are strongest on **process architecture**. They consistently show preliminary screening by classwork or video, followed by richer live stages that may include technique classes, improvisation, solos, workshops, interviews, physical checks or directional response. Ballet-heavy institutions more often observe dancers through class structure and training potential, while contemporary-led institutions more often use workshop, improvisation and discussion structures.

RAD and ISTD provide the most stable **formal descriptor language**. RAD is the strongest formal source for ballet-inflected criteria such as posture, placement, coordination, control, line, timing, musical responsiveness, expression, interpretation and communication. ISTD contributes the most useful cross-style specificity outside ballet: contemporary adds breath, weight, flow, alignment, space use and creative response; modern theatre adds musicality, projection, style/theme, line and space; tap adds clarity of beating, rhythmic interpretation and precision of footwork.

Competition and adjudication frameworks provide **comparator vocabulary**, not direct design rules. They sharpen language on individuality, synchronisation, authenticity, showmanship, audibility and head-to-toe choreography, but they remain competition-shaped and often include logic that cannot be generalised.

Professional company and employer sources are strongest for **actual audition practice**. They show how taped material is used before live stages, what combinations of styles employers ask for, how quickly choreography may be learned before cuts, and how much remains callback-only or room-only. B4 materially improves this evidence base through Candoco, Equity and current cruise/employer calls.

Inclusive-dance and accessibility sources provide the strongest **anti-bias and non-penalisation framework**. They distinguish between changing process and changing standards, support open movement language and adaptation to body or pace, and reject capability assumptions, production-value bias and access-related penalisation.

| Alignment / placement / posture | Organised body placement and postural control | Upper/lower-body organisation, stability, clarity of lines, weight placement | DANCE-S038, DANCE-S041, DANCE-S043 | Exam-board | High | Do not infer injury from deviations |
| Coordination | Integration of limbs, torso, timing and directional clarity | Sequencing, clarity of movement tasks, body-part organisation | DANCE-S017, DANCE-S038, DANCE-S047 | Admissions; exam-board; comparator | High | Competition evidence remains comparator only |
| Control | Managed execution, balance of force, stability and finish | Transitions, dynamic restraint, secure landings, phrase completion | DANCE-S038, DANCE-S041, DANCE-S047 | Exam-board; comparator | High | Generic “good control” is not enough without specifics |

## Technique-specific criteria and observability

### Technique-specific criteria

| Technique/style | Supported criteria | Shared criteria evidenced differently | Observable tape evidence | Live-room-only / exam-room-only / callback-only evidence | Generic feedback risks | Criteria to exclude or avoid | Source ID(s) | Confidence | Evidence gap? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ballet | Placement, line, coordination, control, timing, musical responsiveness, projection, training potential | “Line” and “placement” carry more weight than in some commercial forms | Barre/centre phrase quality, alignment, turnout-related organisation as visible, timing, phrasing | Some class response, pointe screening, physical checks, some live class nuance | “Good technique”, “lovely lines” without specifying placement, timing or control | Body suitability, physique, physical suitability, turnout diagnosis from tape | DANCE-S008, DANCE-S009, DANCE-S038, DANCE-S047, DANCE-S050 | High | Moderate for universal pro-employer transfer |
| Contemporary / modern | Weight, breath, alignment, flow, use of space, improvisation, style/theme, presentation, creative response | “Control” may include yielding, rebound and weight relation rather than held classical control | Floorwork/transitions, weight shifts, dynamic range, spatial use, coherent improvisation if shown | Workshop dialogue, seminar discussion, creative task response in room | “Expressive contemporary” without weight, flow, phrasing or space evidence | Mystique, emotion labels without movement evidence | DANCE-S014, DANCE-S015, DANCE-S041, DANCE-S056, DANCE-S064 | High | Low |
| Jazz / modern theatre | Musicality, projection, line, space use, style/theme, performance quality, quick combo learning | “Performance” and “projection” are more foregrounded than in exam-style ballet documents | Attack, crispness, accents, dynamic timing, style fidelity, presentational clarity | Examiner-set improvisation, combo learning, room response | “Strong performance” without musical or stylistic anchoring | Employer-specific glamour or “look” language | DANCE-S023, DANCE-S042, DANCE-S069, DANCE-S070, DANCE-S071 | Med-High | Moderate |
| Tap | Clarity of beating, precision of footwork, rhythmic interpretation, posture, line/style, audibility | Audibility is more central than in other forms | Footwork clarity, timing, audible beats if captured well, upper-body organisation | Examiner-clapped rhythms, live floor acoustics, room audibility control | “Good rhythm” without specifying beats/precision/audibility | Penalising poor recording capture as poor tap if sound evidence is weak | DANCE-S043, DANCE-S051 | Med-High | Yes — outside exam/adjudication and limited employer evidence |
| Commercial dance | Style responsiveness, camera-awareness, adaptability, speed-learning, versatility, industry-ready phrase clarity | “Professionalism” and “camera translation” enter more often than in exam-board texts | Style fidelity, phrase attack, groove, clarity on camera, brief response | Quick combo learning, long-day consistency, callback direction response | “Commercial look”, “bookable”, “marketable” | Follower count, image, aesthetics, glamour, brand | DANCE-S018, DANCE-S023, DANCE-S059, DANCE-S061, DANCE-S069, DANCE-S070 | Medium | Yes — still partly employer- or practitioner-shaped |
| Street / hip-hop | Groove, musicality, authenticity, full-body choreography, creativity, synchronisation, freestyle/choreography distinction | Authenticity and groove are more central than line/placement | Groove, texture, musical accents, head-to-toe readability, choreographic clarity | Battle logic, live freestyle exchange, callback direction | “Strong swag”, “cool”, “good energy” | Style stereotypes, cultural essentialism, battle-specific logic as universal rule | DANCE-S044, DANCE-S053, DANCE-S069 | Medium | Yes — universal non-competition descriptors remain limited |
| Theatre dance | Style/theme, projection, versatility, musicality, clear presentational intention | Often overlaps with jazz/commercial but with more role/show framing | Phrase execution, presentational clarity, style fit, brief adherence | Show-specific combo learning, staging, partner/context cues | “Stagey”, “strong performer” without movement specifics | Role-specific casting taste as universal standard | DANCE-S042, DANCE-S057, DANCE-S069, DANCE-S072 | Med-High | Moderate |
| Musical Theatre dance | Coordination, musicality, expressive clarity, spatial awareness, mixed-discipline adaptability | More likely to sit alongside acting/singing environment, but dance evidence must stay movement-led | Dance workshop or submitted dance material where present, style clarity, coordination | Mixed-discipline integrated tasks, interviews, singing/acting interplay | “Triple threat” as stand-in for dance evidence | Singing/voice scoring in dance-only contexts | DANCE-S017, DANCE-S021, DANCE-S020 | Medium | Yes — separate dance-only handling required |
